title: The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra
author: Imperially Composed
excerpt: Translated by imperial decree by Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Dharma master of the Kingdom of Khotan under the Great Zhou.

inline.s: Translated by imperial decree by Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda, a Dharma master of the Kingdom of Khotan under the Great Zhou.

blocks.text: Preface to the New Translation of the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra

inline.s: I have heard that the summit of Mount Malaya is the highest and the most majestic, and that the city of Laṅkā is truly hard to reach and hard to enter: it is the ground where the former Buddhas proclaimed the teaching, the place where the sages of old cultivated their practice. And there was a lord of that city, named Rāvaṇa, who rode in his palace to behold the honored countenance; he played music to entreat the wondrous Dharma, using the garlanded peak to express his aspiration and pointing to the ocean of the storehouse to make clear the essential tenet. As for what is called the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra: it is the mysterious pivot of the Buddha-mind of all Buddhas, the wondrous key to the cavern of principles of all the sutras; with ample parables it illumines the hidden purport, with penetrating light it makes the profound meaning clear. It is neither arising nor ceasing, neither existent nor non-existent; it cuts off the two paths of coming and going and is free from the twin attachments of annihilationism and eternalism; through the truth of the supreme meaning one attains the most excellent wondrous jewel. One realizes that all dharmas are empty and that the objects before one are like illusions; one dissolves the distinctions of mere names and equates saṃsāra with nirvāṇa. When Mahāmati first put his question, the purport of the Dharma King was then disclosed: the one hundred and eight meanings accord with ultimate reality and transcend the world, and the thirty-nine gates refute wrong views and proclaim the true Dharma. One comes to understand that names and characteristics are alike provisional and dispels the deluded veil of false imagining; relying on true knowledge one realizes suchness, and awakening to dependent origination one returns to the wondrous principle. When the winds of circumstance have ceased, the waves of consciousness become still; the three self-natures are all empty, the two kinds of selflessness are both extinguished, and one enters the Tathāgata-garbha and roams through the gate of liberation.

This sutra originally came from the Western lands. As for the fact that in the Yuanjia period Guṇabhadra’s translation did not spread abroad, while in the Yanchang period Ratnamati’s rendering of the meaning was in many places mistaken—I reverently pondered the Buddha’s bequest and my heart was earnest to continue and exalt it. In the first year of Jiushi, the year being gengzi, when the pitch-pipe Linzhong was in order and the Yan Emperor held the season, I was then taking refuge from the summer heat at Mount Ji, surveying the manners of the Ying River; and in the Sanyang Palace I once more brought forth this sutra, examining the essential exposition of three versions and completing the fully rounded teaching in seven fascicles. The Tripiṭaka śramaṇa, the Khotanese monk and great worthy Śikṣānanda, together with the monk Fuli of the Great Fuxian Temple and others, all had names that ranked with those of An and Yuan, and virtues that matched those of Teng and Lan; they inherited Nāgārjuna’s fragrant excellence and searched out Aśvaghoṣa’s hidden treasury. The fragrance of their precepts vied with the flower of awakening, and the jewel of their minds was as round as the moon of their nature. Thus they were able to understand the profound and subtle and to unfold the deepest mysteries; and on the fifteenth day of the first month of the fourth year of Chang’an the copying was completed. Thinking myself shallow and unfit, my words no match for the scepter of jade, I look back on the four kinds of eloquence with much shame and gaze upon the One Vehicle and cannot fathom it; yet it was hard to refuse the requests of monastics and laity, and so I have forced myself to set brush to paper. My phrases are clumsy and my exposition awry, and my shame only deepens. I bow to the thought that this sutra is subtle and wondrous, the most rare of all; what I hope is that it may break the darkness of heavy ignorance, that the words of the transmitted lamp may never be exhausted, and that the merit of pouring out its stream, the meaning of the flowing spring, may have no end. The titles of the chapters and their order are set out below.

blocks.text: Chapter One: The Appeal of King Rāvaṇa

inline.s: Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was dwelling on the peak of Mount Malaya, on the shore of the great ocean, in the city of Laṅkā, together with a great assembly of monks and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. All those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had already fully understood the five dharmas, the three self-natures, and the selflessness of the vijñānas; they were skilled in knowing that the objects of their range are the manifestation of their own minds, and they sported in the immeasurable powers of the samādhis, supernormal faculties, and liberations of self-mastery. Manifesting forms of every kind according to the minds of living beings, they tamed and disciplined them with skillful means; all the Buddhas poured water upon their crowns, and they had come to this assembly from lands of Buddhas of every kind, with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati as their foremost.

At that time the World-Honored One was teaching in the palace of the dragon king of the sea. When seven days had passed he came forth from the great ocean, and immeasurable millions of Brahmās, Indras, and world-protectors, together with dragons, devas, and the rest, welcomed the Buddha. Then the Tathāgata raised his eyes and beheld the great city of Laṅkā on Mount Malaya, and at once smiled and spoke these words: “All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Fully Awakened Ones of the past have in this city taught the Dharma of the wisdom of realization that they themselves attained, which is not the range of the conjectures and false views of the non-Buddhists nor the range of the practice of the two vehicles; and I too shall now reveal this Dharma to King Rāvaṇa.” Then Rāvaṇa, king of the yakṣas, by the Buddha’s supernormal power heard the Buddha’s words and knew from afar that the Tathāgata had come forth from the dragon palace, surrounded by Brahmās, Indras, world-protectors, dragons, and devas. Seeing the waves of the ocean and beholding that assembly—the ocean of the ālaya-consciousness stirred by the winds of objectivity, with the waves of the turning consciousnesses rising—he gave rise to a joyful mind and cried aloud in that city: “I shall go to the Buddha and entreat him to enter this city, so that I and all the devas and humans may win great benefit through the long night.” Having spoken these words, he went with his retinue, riding in a flowered palace, to where the World-Honored One was. Arriving there, he descended from the palace and circumambulated him three times, and offered music of every kind as an offering to the Tathāgata. The instruments he held were all of the great blue Indra jewel, inlaid with lapis lazuli and other gems, wrapped about with priceless upper garments; their sound was exquisite and their notes harmonious, and amid it all he spoke verses in praise of the Buddha:
“The Dharma-store of the mind’s own nature, selfless, beyond the stain of views;
That which the wisdom of realization knows—may the Buddha proclaim it for us.
He whose body is a gathering of good dharmas, whose realized wisdom is ever blissful;
He who is master of transformations—may he enter the city of Laṅkā.
Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the past have all dwelt in this city;
And all these hosts of yakṣas wish with one mind to hear the Dharma.”
Then Rāvaṇa, king of Laṅkā, having praised the Buddha in the Tuṭṭaka melody, again spoke in verse, singing:
“For seven days the World-Honored One dwelt in the ocean of Magadha;
Then he came forth from the dragon palace and serenely mounted this shore.
I, with my maidens and the yakṣa retinue,
And Sukhasāra, the wisest among that assembly,
By their supernormal powers all went to where the Tathāgata was,
Each descended from his flower palace and paid reverence to the World-Honored One.
And by the Buddha’s majestic power declared his own name before the Buddha:
‘I am the king of the rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa of the ten heads,
And now I come to where the Buddha is: may the Buddha accept and receive me,
Together with all the living beings within the city of Laṅkā.
Immeasurable Buddhas of the past all ascended the jeweled mountain peak;
Dwelling in the city of Laṅkā, they taught the Dharma they had themselves realized.
So too should the World-Honored One do, dwelling on that jewel-adorned mountain;
Surrounded by the host of bodhisattvas, proclaiming the Dharma of purity.
We, on this very day, together with the host that dwells in Laṅkā,
With one mind all wish to hear the Dharma of realization beyond words.
I recall the Buddhas without measure of the past and future worlds;
Surrounded by bodhisattvas, they proclaimed the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra.
This scripture of the Descent into Laṅkā was praised by the Buddhas of old;
May the Buddha, honored as he goes, unfold it as well for the assembly.
I entreat the Buddha out of compassion for the measureless host of yakṣas:
Enter that jewel-adorned city and teach this wondrous gate of Dharma.
This wondrous city of Laṅkā is adorned with every kind of jewel;
Its walls are not of earth or stone; its netting is all of precious gems.
All these hosts of yakṣas in former times made offerings to the Buddha;
Cultivating practice free of every fault, they know realization clearly and always.
The yakṣas, men and women alike, thirst and long for the Great Vehicle;
They have faith in the Mahāyāna themselves and delight in leading others to abide in it.
We pray the Unsurpassed Honored One, for the sake of all the rākṣasa hosts,
With Kumbhakarṇa and the rest of the retinue, to go to the city of Laṅkā.
Through past, future, and present I have diligently made offerings to the Buddhas;
I wish to hear the Dharma of realization that fulfils the path of the Great Vehicle.
May the Buddha have compassion on me and on all the host of yakṣas;
Together with all the Buddha’s sons, may he enter this city of Laṅkā.
My palaces and my maidens, and all my strings of jewels;
And the lovely Sorrowless Garden—may the Buddha in compassion accept them.
Toward the Buddhas and bodhisattvas there is nothing I would not give;
Even my very body to serve them—I pray you accept it in compassion.’”

Then the World-Honored One, hearing these words, said to him: “King of the yakṣas! In past ages all the great guides, moved by compassion for you, accepted your entreaty and went to the jeweled mountain to teach the Dharma of self-realization; and the Buddhas of the future will do likewise. This is the dwelling place of those who cultivate the profound contemplation and find bliss in the Dharma here and now. Out of compassion for you, I and all the bodhisattvas accept your invitation.” Having spoken these words, he remained silent.

Thereupon King Rāvaṇa offered to the Buddha the wondrous flower palace in which he had come. The Buddha seated himself upon it, and the king with all the bodhisattvas led and followed before and behind, while measureless maidens sang songs of praise; and so they made offerings to the Buddha as they went to that city. When they had reached the city, King Rāvaṇa and all his retinue again made offerings of many kinds, most excellent and wonderful; and the boys and girls among the yakṣa host offered jeweled netting to the Buddha, while King Rāvaṇa gave strings of precious jewels, presenting them to the Buddha and the bodhisattvas to hang about their necks. Then the World-Honored One and all the bodhisattvas, having received these offerings, each briefly taught the profoundly deep Dharma of the realm of self-realization.
Then King Rāvaṇa with his retinue made further offerings to the bodhisattva Mahāmati and entreated him, saying:
“I now entreat you, great being, to put a question to the World-Honored One;
Concerning the realm of the wisdom of realization of all the Tathāgatas.
I, with the yakṣa host and with all these bodhisattvas,
Wish with one mind to hear it; therefore we all entreat you.
You are a cultivator of practice, foremost among speakers;
Therefore we hold you in reverence and entreat you to ask about the Dharma.
The pure Dharma of self-realization, the ultimate entry into the Buddha-ground;
Beyond the non-Buddhists and the two vehicles, beyond all their faults.”

Then the World-Honored One, by his supernormal power, created in that mountain immeasurable jewel mountains besides, all adorned with the wondrous jewels of the heavens in hundreds of thousands of millions, and on every mountain the Buddha’s body appeared; before every Buddha there were King Rāvaṇa and his assembly; and all the lands of the ten directions appeared within them, in every land a Tathāgata, and before every Buddha King Rāvaṇa with his retinue. The great city of Laṅkā and the Aśoka Garden were adorned without any difference, and in each one the bodhisattva Mahāmati rose and put his question, and the Buddha revealed for him the realm of the wisdom of realization, and having taught this sutra with hundreds of thousands of exquisite tones, the Buddha and all the bodhisattvas vanished into the sky and were seen no more.

King Rāvaṇa saw only his own body dwelling in his own palace, and he thought: “Who was it just now? Who heard him speak? What was it that was seen? Who was it that could see? The Buddha, the city, the many jewels, the mountains and groves—where are all these things now? Were they made by a dream? Formed by an illusion? Are they like a city of the gandharvas? Something seen with a cataract? Something conjured by a mirage? Like a barren woman bearing a child in a dream? Like smoke and flame, like a whirling fire-wheel?” And again he thought: “The nature of all dharmas is just like this: it is only the realm of discrimination of one’s own mind. Ordinary people, deluded, cannot understand it. There is none who can see and nothing seen; there is none who can speak and nothing spoken. To see the Buddha and hear the Dharma is all discrimination. As what I just saw cannot see the Buddha, so only when discrimination does not arise can one see.”

Then the king of Laṅkā was at once awakened: he was free from all defilement, realized that there is only the mind itself, and dwelt in non-discrimination. By the power of the wholesome roots he had planted in former times, he attained a vision of all dharmas as they truly are and did not awaken by relying on another. With his own wisdom he could observe with skill, was forever free from all conjecture and false understanding, dwelt in great cultivation as a master of cultivators, manifested bodies of every kind and was thoroughly versed in skillful means, knew well the marks of advancement on the grounds, ever delighted in detachment from mind, intellect, and consciousness, cut off the view of the three continuities, was free from the attachments of the non-Buddhists, awakened inwardly by himself, entered the Tathāgata-garbha, and moved toward the Buddha-ground. He heard voices from the sky and from within the palace, all saying: “Excellent, great king! As you have learned, so should all cultivators learn and so should they see; so should all Tathāgatas see. Whoever sees all dharmas otherwise holds the view of annihilation. You should forever turn away from mind, intellect, and consciousness, should diligently observe all dharmas, should cultivate inner practice and not cling to outer views, and should not fall into the two vehicles or into the non-Buddhists, nor into the meanings of the phrases they cultivate and the realms they see, nor into the samādhis they are said to attain. You should not delight in frivolous talk and laughter, should not give rise to the views of the Vedas, should not cling to the sovereignty of your throne, and should not abide in the six meditations and the like. If you can be thus, then you are practicing as one who cultivates in accordance with reality; you can crush the doctrines of others, can destroy false views, can abandon all attachment to the view of self, can turn the dependent consciousness by wondrous wisdom, can cultivate the path of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattvas, and can enter the Tathāgata’s own realm of realization. You should diligently cultivate and learn in this way, making the Dharma you have attained ever purer; cultivate well the samādhis and the samāpattis, and do not cling to the realms of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists as the highest bliss, as ordinary cultivators discriminate it. The non-Buddhists, grasping at a self, hold the view that there is a self, and grasping at real qualities they give rise to attachment; those of the two vehicles see existence and non-existence, ignorance and its conditions, and in the emptiness of nature they give rise to confused discrimination. King of Laṅkā! This Dharma is supreme: it is the path of the Great Vehicle, and it can bring one to accomplish the noble wisdom of self-realization and to receive a most wondrous birth among the realms of existence. King of Laṅkā! This practice of the Great Vehicle destroys the cataract of ignorance, extinguishes the waves of the consciousnesses, and does not fall into the crooked practices of the non-Buddhists. King of Laṅkā! Non-Buddhist practitioners, clinging to a self, produce various strange doctrines and cannot expound the two meanings of being free from attachment, of seeing consciousness, and of the nature of that which is seen. Excellent, king of Laṅkā! When you first saw the Buddha and pondered this meaning—such pondering is itself seeing the Buddha.”

Then King Rāvaṇa again thought: “May I once more be granted to behold the Tathāgata! The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is master of contemplation, is free from the dharmas of the non-Buddhists, can teach the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, surpasses all that the transformation bodies ought to do, dwells in the Tathāgata’s meditative absorption and enters the bliss of samādhi; therefore he is called the great master of contemplation, and is also named the greatly compassionate one, who can burn up the faggots of affliction and discrimination until they are gone, who is surrounded by the assembly of the Buddha’s sons, who enters into the minds of all living beings, who pervades every place and possesses all wisdom, and who is forever free from all marks of discrimination. I now pray that I may see again the Tathāgata’s great supernormal power; and by seeing it, what I have not attained I may attain and what I have attained may not fall away, and free from all discrimination I may dwell in the bliss of samādhi and increase and fulfil the Tathāgata’s ground of wisdom.”

Then the World-Honored One, knowing that the king of Laṅkā was about to realize the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, manifested his body out of compassion and caused all that he had created to return to what it had been. Then the ten-headed king beheld what he had seen before: immeasurable mountain cities all adorned with jewels, and in every city a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Fully Awakened One, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks. He saw his own body before all the Buddhas; all had Mahāmati, surrounded by yakṣas, teaching the Dharma of the range of the wisdom of realization; and he also saw the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, all such things without any difference.

Then the World-Honored One surveyed the whole assembly, gazing with the eye of wisdom and not with the eye of flesh, and like a lion roused to vigor he turned his glance and laughed joyfully. From the mark between his brows, from his thighs, his sides, his waist and neck, from his shoulders and arms, and from the mark upon his breast, from every pore he sent forth immeasurable rays of wondrous color, like a rainbow trailing radiance, like the sun spreading its light, like the fierce blaze of the fire at the end of an aeon. Then Brahmā, Indra, and the four heavenly kings in the sky saw from afar the Tathāgata seated on the peak of Mount Laṅkā like Mount Sumeru, laughing joyfully. Then all the bodhisattvas and all the hosts of devas thought: “The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is master of the Dharma—for what reason does he laugh joyfully? His body sends forth light and he sits silent and unmoving, dwelling in the realm of self-realization and entering the bliss of samādhi, like a lion turning his head to look about him, beholding Rāvaṇa and contemplating the Dharma of reality.”

Then the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati, who had first received the entreaty of King Rāvaṇa, and who also knew the minds of the assembly of bodhisattvas, and who further beheld how all living beings in the future would delight in clinging to words and letters, grasping at the meaning according to the words and so giving rise to delusion, and would hold to the practices of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists—or who would think: “The World-Honored One is already beyond the realms of the consciousnesses; for what reason does he laugh joyfully?”—put his question to the Buddha in order to cut off their doubt.

The Buddha said to him: “Excellent, Mahāmati! Excellent, Mahāmati! You look upon the world and take pity on living beings, who through the three times are bound by evil views, and wishing to awaken them you have put this question to me. The wise, for the benefit of themselves and others, are able to ask such a question. Mahāmati! This king of Laṅkā once asked all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Fully Awakened Ones of the past about the meaning of the two kinds; he wishes to ask about it now as well, and so will he in the future. The marks of difference between these two meanings cannot be fathomed by any of the two vehicles or by the non-Buddhists.”

Then the Tathāgata, knowing that the king of Laṅkā wished to ask this meaning, said to him: “King of Laṅkā! If you wish to ask me, you should ask quickly. I shall explain it for you in detail, fulfil your wish and make you glad. You will be able to contemplate and observe with wisdom, free from all discrimination, well knowing the grounds and the cultivation of their remedies; you will realize the true meaning and enter the bliss of samādhi, be received by all Tathāgatas, dwell in the bliss of śamatha, be far from the faults of the samādhis of the two vehicles, and abide on the ground of the bodhisattva of unshakable good wisdom and the Dharma-cloud. You will be able to know all dharmas as they truly are, as without self; and in the great palace of the jewel lotus you will be consecrated with the water of samādhi. There will appear immeasurable lotus flowers all around, and countless bodhisattvas dwelling among them, gazing at one another with the whole assembly: such a realm is inconceivable. King of Laṅkā! If you rouse a single practice of skillful means and abide on the ground of cultivation, and rouse immeasurable practices of skillful means besides, you will surely attain the inconceivable things spoken of above, dwell in the Tathāgata’s position, and respond to beings according to their forms. What you are to attain has never been seen by any of the two vehicles, by the non-Buddhists, by Brahmā and Indra, or by the devas.”

Then the king of Laṅkā, having received the Buddha’s permission, rose from his seat on the peak of the jewel mountain of pure radiance, as luminous as a great lotus, surrounded by the host of his maidens, and created immeasurable flowers of every color, perfumes, incenses, and unguents of every color and fragrance, banners, canopies, and curtains, crowns and pendants and strings of jewels, and all the other wondrous and excellent adornments never seen or heard in the world; and he further created all the immeasurable musical instruments of the desire realm, surpassing all that the devas, dragons, gandharvas, and all the rest of the world possess; and he further created the musical instruments seen in former times in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; and he further created a great jeweled net covering all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas; and he further manifested all kinds of wondrous garments and set up banners and canopies as offerings. Having done these things, he rose into the sky to the height of seven tāla trees; and in the sky he again rained down clouds of offerings of every kind and made music, and coming down from the sky he seated himself on the peak of the jewel mountain called Sunlight of the Second Day, which is like a great lotus, and joyfully and reverently spoke these words: “I now wish to ask the Tathāgata about the two meanings. These two meanings I have already asked the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Fully Awakened Ones of the past, and those World-Honored Ones have already explained them to me. Now I wish to ask about this meaning as well; may the Tathāgata proclaim it for me. World-Honored One! It is the Buddhas of transformation who teach these two meanings, not the fundamental Buddha. The fundamental Buddha teaches the realm of the bliss of samādhi and does not teach the range of false discrimination. Excellent, World-Honored One, who are master of the Dharma! May you in compassion teach these two meanings, which all the Buddha’s sons long in their hearts to hear.”

Then the World-Honored One said to that king: “You should ask, and I shall explain it for you.” Then the yakṣa king, putting on yet more crowns of jewels and strings of pearls and all kinds of adornments to deck his body, spoke these words: “The Tathāgata has always taught: ‘The Dharma itself is to be abandoned, how much more what is not Dharma.’ How then can these two dharmas be abandoned? Which is Dharma, and which is not Dharma? If the Dharma is to be abandoned, how can there be two? If there are two, then one falls into the marks of discrimination. That there is a substance or no substance, that a thing is real or unreal—all of this is discrimination, and one cannot understand the markless sameness of the ālaya-consciousness. As a hair-wheel appears where there is no pure realm of wisdom, so is the Dharma-nature: how can it be abandoned?”

Then the Buddha said to the king of Laṅkā: “King of Laṅkā! Do you not see such impermanent and perishing things as a pot, in which ordinary people falsely give rise to discrimination? Why do you not in the same way understand the marks of difference between Dharma and non-Dharma? These are what ordinary people discriminate; they are not the vision of realized wisdom. Ordinary people fall among marks of every kind; those who have realized do not. King of Laṅkā! When a palace or a garden burns, one sees flames of every kind, yet the nature of fire is one; the light and flames it sends forth differ in length and size each according to the strength of the fuel. Why do you not in the same way understand the marks of difference between Dharma and non-Dharma? King of Laṅkā! As a single seed produces a sprout, a stalk, branches, leaves, and immeasurable differences of flowers and fruit, so it is with outer dharmas, and so it is with inner dharmas too. It is said that ignorance as condition produces all dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; and within the three realms beings receive birth in the various destinies, with differences of suffering and pleasure, beauty and ugliness, speech and silence, movement and rest. And as the marks of the consciousnesses, though one, have, according to their objects, differences of superior, middling, and inferior, defiled and pure, good and evil—King of Laṅkā! Not only do dharmas such as these have differences: when cultivators practice contemplation, even the range of their own wisdom is seen to have marks of difference, how much more do Dharma and non-Dharma have all kinds of difference and discrimination. King of Laṅkā! You should know that the marks of difference between Dharma and non-Dharma are all due to the discrimination of marks.

“King of Laṅkā! What is Dharma? It is that the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists falsely discriminate and say that there are real entities and the like as the causes of dharmas: such dharmas as these should be abandoned and forsaken, and one should not discriminate and grasp marks within them. When one sees the Dharma-nature of one’s own mind, then there is no attachment; pots and other things, which the foolish grasp at, are from the first without substance. The practitioners of contemplation, observing truly with insight (vipaśyanā), are said to abandon all dharmas. King of Laṅkā! What is non-Dharma? It is that all dharmas are without nature and without marks, forever beyond discrimination: for one who sees truly, such realms as existence and non-existence do not arise at all, and this is called abandoning non-Dharma. There is further non-Dharma: the hare’s horn, the child of a barren woman, and the like, which are all without nature or marks and cannot be discriminated, and are spoken of as having names only in accordance with worldly convention; they are not like a pot, which can be grasped and clung to, because they are not objects of consciousness. Such discrimination as this should also be abandoned: this is called abandoning Dharma and abandoning non-Dharma. King of Laṅkā! What you asked before, I have now explained.”

“King of Laṅkā! You say: ‘I have already asked this meaning of the Tathāgatas of the past, and those Tathāgatas have explained it to me.’ King of Laṅkā! What you call the past is only discrimination; so too is the future, and I am the same as they. King of Laṅkā! The Dharma of those Buddhas is altogether beyond discrimination and has gone beyond all the idle talk of discrimination; it is not like a mark of form, and only wisdom can realize it. It is in order to bring living beings to peace and happiness that they proclaim the Dharma, and because they teach with the wisdom of no marks they are called Tathāgatas. Therefore the Tathāgata has wisdom as his substance; and because wisdom is his body, he cannot be discriminated, cannot be the object of discrimination, cannot be discriminated by the marks of self, person, or living being. Why can he not be discriminated? Because consciousness arises depending on objects and grasps at marks of form and color; therefore he is free from the act of discrimination and free from what is discriminated. King of Laṅkā! It is like painted figures of living beings on a wall: they have no awareness. So too are all living beings in the world: without karma and without reward, and so too are all dharmas: nothing to hear and nothing to speak. King of Laṅkā! Living beings in the world are like magical transformations, which ordinary people and the non-Buddhists cannot understand. King of Laṅkā! To be able to see in this way is called right view; any other view is called the view of discrimination, and because of discrimination one grasps at duality.

“King of Laṅkā! Suppose a man sees his own image in water or in a mirror, sees his own shadow in a lamp or in the moon, or hears his own echo in a valley, and thereupon gives rise to discrimination and becomes attached: so it is here as well. Dharma and non-Dharma are only discrimination, and because of discrimination one cannot abandon them, but only increases all that is false and does not attain cessation. What is called cessation is the single condition, and the single condition is the most excellent samādhi. From it the noble wisdom of self-realization can arise, taking the Tathāgata-garbha as its range.”

blocks.text: Chapter Two, Part One: The Gathering of All Dharmas

inline.s: Then the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati, together with the bodhisattva Mati, who had journeyed through all the Buddha-lands, rose from his seat by the Buddha’s supernormal power, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, bowed in reverence, and spoke these verses:
“The world is free from birth and death, like a flower in empty space;
Wisdom does not fall into being or non-being, and yet great compassion arises.
All dharmas are like illusions, far removed from mind and consciousness;
The world is ever like a dream, far removed from annihilation and permanence;
Knowing persons and dharmas to be selfless, and afflictions and their objects;
Ever pure and without marks, and yet great compassion arises.
The Buddha does not dwell in nirvāṇa, nor nirvāṇa in the Buddha;
Beyond the awakened and the unawakened, whether one says there is or there is not.
The dharmakāya is like an illusion, a dream—how can it be praised?
To know that there is no nature and no arising: this alone is called praising the Buddha.
The Buddha has no marks of sense or object, and not seeing him is called seeing the Buddha;
How can there be praise or blame in regard to the Muni?
One who sees the Muni as still and far removed from arising,
Such a one, in this life and the next, is free from attachment and sees nothing.”
Then the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati, having praised the Buddha in verse, declared his own name:
“My name is Mahāmati; I have penetrated the Great Vehicle;
Now with a hundred and eight meanings I look up and ask the honored among the honored.”
Then the World-Understanding One, hearing these words, surveyed the whole assembly and spoke:
“You sons of the Buddha, ask now whatever you wish;
I shall explain for you the realm of self-realization.”
Then the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati, having received the Buddha’s permission, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet and asked in verse:
“How does conceptualization arise? How is conceptualization purified?
How does delusion arise? How is delusion purified?
What is it to be a son of the Buddha, and what are the shadowless stages?
How are the lands transformed? What of the marks, and the non-Buddhists?
Where does liberation lead? Who is bound, and who can loose the bond?
What is the realm of dhyāna? For what reason are there three vehicles?
From what cause are they born? What acts, and what can act?
Who declares that both are different? How do the various existences arise?
What is the formless absorption, and the absorption of cessation?
What is the cessation of perception? How does one awake from absorption?
How is birth brought about by action, and how does one move on and maintain the body?
How does one see things? How does one enter the stages?
How is one a son of the Buddha? Who can break through the three existences?
Where is the body, and of what kind? Once born, where does it dwell?
How are supernormal powers attained, and mastery, and samādhi?
What is the mark of the mind in samādhi? May the Buddha explain it for me.
What is called the ālaya-consciousness? What is called the mental consciousness?
How do the views arise? How are the views abandoned?”
How is the name no-name? How is it mind-only?
By what cause are marks set up? How is non-self attained?
How is there no being? How is one spoken of in worldly terms?
How does one come to non-arising, and to views of permanence and of annihilation?
How do the Buddha and the heterodox not oppose each other in their marks?
Why will there be, in ages to come, so many and various schools?
How is it that nature is empty? How is it that there is momentary destruction?
How does the womb-store arise? How is the world unmoved?
How are all the worlds illusory and dream-like,
a city of the gandharvas, a mirage, even the moon in the water?
What are the factors of enlightenment? From where do the limbs of awakening arise?
How is a land in disorder? Why are the realms of existence seen?
How does one know the worldly Dharma? How is one free from words?
How is it like a flower in the sky, neither arising nor ceasing?
How many kinds of suchness are there? How many minds in the perfections?
How is one like space? How is one free from discrimination?
What is the sequence of the grounds? How does one attain the shadowless?
What are the two kinds of non-self? How is the knowable purified?
How many kinds of noble wisdom are there? And of the moral discipline of beings?
The mani and all such jewels, from where do they all come forth?
Who gives rise to speech, to beings, and to all things?
The branches of learning and the arts, by whom are they revealed?
How many kinds of gāthā are there? And of long-line prose and verses?
How many different principles are there? How many kinds of explanation?
Who is it that makes food and drink? How does desire arise?
What of the wheel-turning king? And of all the lesser kings?
How are kings guarded? How many kinds of heavenly hosts are there?
Earth, sun, moon, and stars, what are all these?
How many kinds of liberation are there? How many kinds of spiritual teachers?
What is an ācārya? How many kinds of disciples are there?
How many kinds of Tathāgata are there? And of the stories of former lives?
The demons and the heterodox, how many of each are there?
How many different kinds of self-nature are there? How many kinds of mind?
How is it mere designation? Pray, Buddha, reveal it to us.
How do wind and cloud arise? From what cause come mindfulness and wisdom?
The rows of creepers and trees, who is it that makes them all?
How do elephants, horses, and beasts arise? For what reason are they caught?
How does one become a lowly person? Who is it that makes all these?
How are the six periods embraced? How is one an icchantika?
Women, men, and the neuter, how are all these born?
How does practice advance? How does practice fall back?
How many kinds of yogin are there? One causes beings to dwell therein.
Beings are born in all the destinies: what form, what colour and shape?
Great wealth and great mastery, by what cause are they obtained?
What is the lineage of the Śākyas? What is the lineage of the cane?
The seers who practise long austerities, whose teaching is that?
For what cause does the World-Honored Buddha appear in every land,
of various names and every kind of form, surrounded by the Buddha's sons?
For what cause does one not eat meat? For what cause is meat to be abandoned?
The beings that eat meat, for what cause do they eat it?
Why are the lands shaped like the sun and the moon,
like Sumeru and the lotus, like the swastika and the lion?
Why are the lands like Indra's net,
covered or lying on their sides, all made of every kind of jewel?
Why do the lands have the stainless light of sun and moon,
or the shape of a flower or a fruit, a harp, or a narrow-waisted drum?
What is a Buddha of transformation? What is a Buddha of reward?
What is the Buddha of suchness and wisdom? Pray tell me all of this.
Why is supreme perfect enlightenment not attained in the realm of desire?
Why is bodhi won, free from defilement, at the summit of form?
After the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa, who will uphold the true Dharma?
How long will the World-Honored One abide? How long will the true Dharma remain?
How many kinds of siddhānta are there? How many views are there?
Why was the Vinaya established, and the community of bhikṣus,
all the Buddha's sons, the solitary realizers, and the hearers?
How is the support turned about? How is the signless attained?
How are worldly powers attained? How does one transcend the world?
And for what reason does the mind dwell in the seventh ground?
How many kinds of saṅgha are there? How is a schism in the saṅgha brought about?
Why, for the sake of beings, are medical treatises widely taught?
Why does the great Muni proclaim a saying such as this:
‘Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni are myself’?
Why is annihilation and permanence taught, and self and non-self?
Why is it not always taught that all is only mind?
How do the groves of men and women, the haritakī and āmra trees,
Mount Kailāsa, the circular mountain wall, and the vajra mountains,
and the space between them, adorned with boundless jewels,
all filled with seers and gandharvas:
for what cause are all these? Pray, Honored One, tell me.’

Then the World-Honored One, hearing his request for the wondrous Mahāyāna, the supreme Dharma-gate of the mind of all Buddhas, spoke to him thus: ‘Excellent, Mahāmati! Listen well, listen well! As you have asked, so will I set it forth in order.’ And he spoke these verses:
“Whether born or unborn, nirvāṇa and the mark of emptiness,
revolving with no self-nature, the pāramitās, the Buddha's sons,
the hearers, the solitary realizers, and the formless course of the heterodox.
Sumeru and the great ocean mountains, the continents and the lands,
the stars with the sun and moon, the gods and the asuras,
liberation, mastery, and superknowledges, the powers, the dhyānas, the samādhis.
Cessation and the bases of success, the limbs of enlightenment and the path,
the dhyānas and the immeasurables, the aggregates and coming and going,
even the cessation attainments, the mind giving rise to speech,
mind, mentation, and consciousness as non-self, the five dharmas and self-nature.
The discriminated and the discriminating, the two views of grasped and grasper;
the lineage and the sphere of the several vehicles, gold, mani, and pearl.
The icchantika and the great elements, the wilderness of disorder, and one Buddha;
the known, the knowing, the teaching attained, and beings' existence and non-existence.
For what cause elephants, horses, and beasts? How are they caught?
By what reason and analogy is a siddhānta made to accord?
The made and the maker, the many groves and delusion;
such is the true principle: mind only, with no objective realm.
The grounds have no sequence; the signless turns the support about;
medical treatises and arts and crafts, the crafts and all the branches of learning.
Sumeru and the mountain ranges, the great ocean, the sun and moon, their measure;
beings above, between, and below: how many atoms in each body?
How many atoms in each land, how many cubits in each bow's length;
how many bows in a krośa, in half a yojana, in a yojana?
The hare's hair and the mote in a gap, the louse's egg, sheep's wool, barley grains;
half a pint and one pint, how many barley grains is each?
One bushel and ten bushels, a hundred thousand and a thousand million;
and so on up to the bimbara: how many are each of these?
How many atoms make a mustard seed? How many mustard seeds make a grass seed?
And how many grass seeds make a single bean?
How many beans make a farthing's weight? How many farthings make an ounce?
How many ounces make a pound? How many pounds make Sumeru?
These are what you should have asked: why ask about other matters?
The hearers and solitary realizers, the Buddhas and the Buddha's sons,
the measure of each such body: how many atoms has each?
How many atoms in fire and wind? How many in each sense-faculty?
The brows and all the hair-pores: of how many atoms is each made?
Such matters as these: why do you not ask me of them?
How is wealth obtained? How does one become a wheel-turning king?
How are kings guarded? How is liberation attained?
How do the statements of the long prose run, of lust and of food and drink,
And how of men and women’s groves? Of Mount Vajra and the rest,
Illusion, dream, and thirsting love—whence do the clouds all rise?
Why do the seasons come to be? What makes the many tastes?
Women and men, and neuter too, adorned by Buddhas and by bodhisattvas,
How are the wondrous mountains made, adorned by rishis and gandharvas?
Where does liberation lead? Who binds, and who is set free?
What is the realm of dhyana? Transformation, and the non-Buddhist paths,
How do things arise without a cause? How do they arise from causes?
How are the various views overturned? How does conceptual thought arise?
What is pure conceptualizing? How do created things arise?
How does one pass away? How are the various thoughts cut off?
How is samadhi entered? Who breaks the three realms of existence?
Where does the body dwell, and what is it? How is there no self?
Why speak in keeping with convention? What are the marks you ask about?
And the selflessness you ask of—how is there the tathagata-garbha,
And how the other branches too? How is eternalism cut off, and nihilism?
How is the mind one-pointed? What is the wisdom of speech?
Sons of the Buddha of the precepts’ lineage—how are they expounded in accord with truth?
How are teacher and disciple, and the different natures of beings?
Food and drink, and space, the clever and the Mara’s constructs—
How are the trees laid out in rows? This is what you ask.
For what reason do all the lands have such different appearances?
Some are like the konghou lute, the waist-drum, and a host of flowers;
Some are without light, where rishis undergo long austerities;
Some have noble clans and lineages, making beings hold them in respect.
Some have bodies low and mean, despised by other people;
Why, in the realm of desire, does one practice yet not attain Buddhahood,
While in the highest heaven of form one rises to perfect enlightenment?
How can people of the world obtain supernormal powers?
For what reason is one called a bhikshu? For what reason is one called the sangha?
How are the emanation body and the reward body, the Tathagata of true suchness and of wisdom?
How is one’s mind made to abide in the seventh ground?
This, and the other meanings besides, you now ask me.
As the Buddhas of old have taught, there are one hundred and eight statements;
Each corresponds to the next, transcending all wrong views.
They are beyond the worldly too—dharmas constructed by words and speech;
I shall now expound them for you; sons of the Buddha, you should listen and receive.”
Then Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what are these one hundred and eight statements?”

The Buddha said: “Mahamati, they are: the statement of birth and the statement of no birth; the statement of permanence and the statement of no permanence; the statement of characteristic and the statement of no characteristic; the statement of dwelling and difference and the statement of no dwelling and difference; the statement of the moment and the statement of no moment; the statement of own-nature and the statement of no own-nature; the statement of emptiness and the statement of no emptiness; the statement of annihilation and the statement of no annihilation; the statement of mind and the statement of no mind; the statement of the middle and the statement of no middle; the statement of condition and the statement of no condition; the statement of cause and the statement of no cause; the statement of affliction and the statement of no affliction; the statement of craving and the statement of no craving; the statement of skillful means and the statement of no skillful means; the statement of skill in means and the statement of no skill in means; the statement of purity and the statement of no purity; the statement of correspondence and the statement of no correspondence; the statement of simile and the statement of no simile; the statement of disciple and the statement of no disciple; the statement of teacher and the statement of no teacher; the statement of lineage and the statement of no lineage; the statement of the three vehicles and the statement of no three vehicles; the statement of no reflected image and the statement of no absence of reflected image; the statement of vow and the statement of no vow; the statement of the three wheels and the statement of no three wheels; the statement of marking and the statement of no marking; the statement of existence and the statement of no existence; the statement of nonexistence and the statement of no nonexistence; the statement of both and the statement of neither; the statement of self-realized noble wisdom and the statement of no self-realized noble wisdom; the statement of the bliss of the present Dharma and the statement of no bliss of the present Dharma; the statement of a land and the statement of no land; the statement of a dust-mote and the statement of no dust-mote; the statement of water and the statement of no water; the statement of a bow and the statement of no bow; the statement of the great elements and the statement of no great elements; the statement of calculation and the statement of no calculation; the statement of supernormal powers and the statement of no supernormal powers; the statement of space and the statement of no space; the statement of a cloud and the statement of no cloud; the statement of the sciences and the statement of no sciences; the statement of crafts and the statement of no crafts; the statement of wind and the statement of no wind; the statement of earth and the statement of no earth; the statement of mind and the statement of no mind; the statement of provisional positing and the statement of no provisional positing; the statement of essential nature and the statement of no essential nature; the statement of the aggregates and the statement of no aggregates; the statement of beings and the statement of no beings; the statement of awakening and the statement of no awakening; the statement of nirvāṇa and the statement of no nirvāṇa; the statement of the knowable and the statement of no knowable; the statement of non-Buddhist paths and the statement of no non-Buddhist paths; the statement of confusion and the statement of no confusion; the statement of illusion and the statement of no illusion; the statement of dream and the statement of no dream; the statement of the mirage and the statement of no mirage; the statement of reflected image and the statement of no reflected image; the statement of the fire-wheel and the statement of no fire-wheel; the statement of the gandharva and the statement of no gandharva; the statement of a god and the statement of no god; the statement of food and drink and the statement of no food and drink; the statement of lust and the statement of no lust; the statement of a view and the statement of no view; the statement of the paramitas and the statement of no paramitas; the statement of precepts and the statement of no precepts; the statement of sun, moon, and stars and the statement of no sun, moon, and stars; the statement of truth and the statement of no truth; the statement of fruit and the statement of no fruit; the statement of cessation and the statement of no cessation; the statement of cessation and arising and the statement of no cessation and arising; the statement of medicine and the statement of no medicine; the statement of characteristic and the statement of no characteristic; the statement of constituent parts and the statement of no constituent parts; the statement of dhyana and the statement of no dhyana; the statement of delusion and the statement of no delusion; the statement of manifestation and the statement of no manifestation; the statement of protection and the statement of no protection; the statement of lineage and the statement of no lineage; the statement of the rishis and the statement of no rishis; the statement of a king and the statement of no king; the statement of acceptance and the statement of no acceptance; the statement of a jewel and the statement of no jewel; the statement of prophecy and the statement of no prophecy; the statement of the icchantika and the statement of no icchantika; the statement of women, men, and neuters and the statement of no women, men, and neuters; the statement of taste and the statement of no taste; the statement of action and the statement of no action; the statement of body and the statement of no body; the statement of conceptualizing and the statement of no conceptualizing; the statement of movement and the statement of no movement; the statement of faculties and the statement of no faculties; the statement of the conditioned and the statement of no conditioned; the statement of cause and effect and the statement of no cause and effect; the statement of the highest heaven of form and the statement of no highest heaven of form; the statement of seasons and the statement of no seasons; the statement of trees and vines and the statement of no trees and vines; the statement of the various and the statement of no various; the statement of exposition and the statement of no exposition; the statement of determination and the statement of no determination; the statement of the Vinaya and the statement of no Vinaya; the statement of the bhikshu and the statement of no bhikshu; the statement of dharma-preservation and the statement of no dharma-preservation. Mahamati, these one hundred and eight statements are what all the Buddhas of the past have taught (two entries are missing from this enumeration; they should be sought elsewhere).”
Then Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, dwelling, and ceasing do the various consciousnesses have?”

The Buddha said: “Mahamati, the various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, dwelling, and ceasing, which those who conjecture cannot know. They are: the continuance-arising and the mark-arising, the continuance-dwelling and the mark-dwelling, the continuance-ceasing and the mark-ceasing. The various consciousnesses have three marks: the mark of turning, the mark of karma, and the mark of truth. Mahamati, consciousness is spoken of extensively as eight, but in brief as only two: the manifesting consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates objects. Mahamati, as all forms appear in a bright mirror, so it is with the manifesting consciousness. Mahamati, the manifesting consciousness and the consciousness that discriminates objects are not two different consciousnesses; each is the cause of the other. Mahamati, the manifesting consciousness takes inconceivable permeation and transformation as its cause; the consciousness that discriminates objects takes the discriminated objects and the habit-energy of beginningless conceptual play as its cause. Mahamati, when the various habit-energies of the alaya-consciousness’s false discrimination cease, then all the sense consciousnesses cease: this is called mark-ceasing. Mahamati, as for continuance-ceasing, when the supporting cause ceases and the object ceases, then continuance ceases. The supporting cause is the false habit-energy of beginningless conceptual play. The object is the discriminated objects seen by one’s own mind. Mahamati, for example, a lump of clay and a dust-mote are neither different nor not different; so too are gold and its ornaments. Mahamati, if the lump of clay and the dust-mote were different, the one could not be made of the other; but it is made of it, and so they are not different. If they were not different, the lump of clay and the dust-mote would be indistinguishable. Mahamati, if the turning consciousness and the storehouse consciousness were different, the storehouse consciousness would not be their cause; if they were not different, when the turning consciousness ceased the storehouse consciousness would cease too—yet its mark of truth does not cease. Mahamati, the mark of truth of consciousness does not cease; only the mark of karma ceases. If the mark of truth ceased, the storehouse consciousness would cease; and if the storehouse consciousness ceased, that would be no different from the non-Buddhist doctrine of annihilation.

“Mahamati, those non-Buddhists speak in this way: ‘When the consciousness that continues by grasping objects ceases, the beginningless continuing consciousness ceases.’ Mahamati, those non-Buddhists say that the continuing consciousness is born from a creator, and do not say that the eye-consciousness arises from the coming together of form, light, and attention; they say only that the creator is the productive cause. What is the creator? They reckon that the primal nature, the person, the sovereign, time, and the dust-motes are the makers. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are seven kinds of own-nature: the own-nature of accumulation, the own-nature of nature, the own-nature of characteristic, the own-nature of the great elements, the own-nature of cause, the own-nature of condition, and the own-nature of completion. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are seven kinds of supreme meaning: the range of mind, the range of wisdom, the range of dualistic views, the range transcending dualistic views, the range transcending the stage of the sons of the Buddha, the range of the Tathagata, and the range of the Tathagata’s self-realized noble wisdom. Mahamati, this is the supreme meaning mind, the Dharma own-nature of all Tathagatas, worthy ones, and perfectly enlightened ones of past, future, and present; by this mind they accomplish the supreme dharmas of the world and beyond the world of a Tathagata, and with the noble wisdom-eye they enter the various positing of shared and individual characteristics, and their positing is not shared with the evil views of non-Buddhists. Mahamati, what is the evil view of non-Buddhists? It is not knowing that objects appear through one’s own discrimination, and so, regarding own-nature and supreme meaning, seeing existence and seeing nonexistence and giving rise to speech about them. Mahamati, I shall now teach that if one understands objects to be like illusions, appearing from one’s own mind, then one extinguishes deluded thought, the suffering of the three realms of existence, and the causes and conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma.

“Mahamati, there are shramanas and brahmans who wrongly reckon that things appear outside of cause and effect as existent or nonexistent, abiding according to time; or they reckon that the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields arise and dwell dependent on conditions, and once existent, cease. Mahamati, for them, whether continuance, function, arising, ceasing, the various realms of existence, nirvāṇa, the path, karma, fruit, or truth—this is a doctrine of destruction and annihilation. Why? Because they do not attain the present Dharma and do not see the root. Mahamati, for example, when a bottle is broken it no longer serves as a bottle, and a scorched seed cannot sprout; so it is here. If the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields appear and then cease, one should know that there is no continuance-arising, since there is no cause; it is merely what one’s own mind falsely sees.

“Furthermore, Mahamati, if originally there were no consciousness arising from the coming together of the three conditions, then a tortoise should grow hair and sand should yield oil; your thesis would be ruined and would contradict established meanings, and all your works would be empty and without benefit. Mahamati, the coming together of the three as condition is the nature of cause and effect and may be spoken of as existent. That past, present, and future arise from nothing is what those who dwell on the stage of awakened imagination, together with all their reasoning and teaching and the residual habit-energy of their own evil views, say. Mahamati, foolish ordinary beings, devoured by evil views and drunk on wrong views, lacking wisdom, falsely claim to speak as all-knowing ones.

“Mahamati, there are further shramanas and brahmans who contemplate all dharmas as without own-nature, like clouds in the sky, like a wheel of fire, like a gandharva city, like an illusion, like a mirage, like the moon in water, like things seen in a dream, never apart from one’s own mind; because of beginningless false seeing they take them as external. Having contemplated thus, they cut off the conditions of discrimination and are free of the names and meanings grasped by deluded mind; they know that body and possessions and the places where they dwell are all the range of the storehouse consciousness, with no grasping or grasped, no arising, dwelling, or ceasing; thus they think and abide without letting go. Mahamati, such a bodhisattva-mahasattva will before long attain the equality of samsara and nirvāṇa, the effortless course of great compassion and skillful means, contemplate beings as illusions and shadows arising from conditions, know that all objects are unattainable apart from mind, walk the path of no characteristics and gradually ascend the grounds, dwell in the realm of samadhi, thoroughly understand that the three realms are only one’s own mind, attain the samadhi of illusion and cut off all reflected images, accomplish wisdom and realize the dharma of non-arising; entering the samadhi that is like a diamond, they will attain the Buddha body, forever dwell in suchness, and give rise to the powers, supernormal faculties, and mastery of various transformations. Mahamati, adorned with skillful means they journey through the many Buddha lands, free of non-Buddhist paths and of mind, intellect, and consciousness, and in due order of turning they accomplish the Tathagata body. Mahamati, a bodhisattva-mahasattva who wishes to attain the Buddha body should keep far from the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, mind, conditions, and the arisen, dwelling, and ceasing dharmas of the constructed, and from conceptual discrimination; they should dwell only in the measure of mind, observe the three realms, and, since they arise from beginningless false habit, contemplate the Tathagata ground’s markless, non-arising, self-realized noble Dharma; they attain mastery of mind and effortless course, and like a wish-fulfilling jewel appear in forms as suited, leading others to understand mind-only and gradually enter the grounds. Therefore, Mahamati, a bodhisattva-mahasattva should well cultivate and learn their own tradition.”

blocks.text: Chapter on the Collection of All Dharmas, Part Two of Two

inline.s: Then Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I pray you teach me the wonderful Dharma-gate of mind, intellect, and consciousness and of the five dharmas and own-natures, which is the entry of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas into the range of their own minds, beyond the marks of any course of action, and which accords with true meaning, the Buddha-mind of all Buddhas. I pray the Tathagata, for the sake of the bodhisattvas in this mountain assembly, following the Buddhas of the past, will expound the realm of the dharmakaya in the ocean waves of the storehouse consciousness.”

Then the World-Honored One said to Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva: “There are four conditions by which the eye-consciousness turns. What are the four? They are: not awakening to one’s own mind’s appearing and so grasping at it; the false habit-energy of beginninglessly grasping at form; the intrinsic nature of consciousness being thus; and delighting in seeing the various forms. Mahamati, by these four conditions the alaya-consciousness, like a rushing torrent, gives rise to the waves of the turning consciousnesses. As with the eye-consciousness, so with the rest. In all the faculties, dust-motes, and pores—eye and so forth—the turning consciousnesses may arise all at once, as a bright mirror shows all forms, or may arise gradually, as a fierce wind stirs the waters of the great ocean. So too with the ocean of mind: the wind of objects stirs up the waves of the consciousnesses without ceasing. Mahamati, the marks produced by karma are neither one nor different; karma and the marks of birth are bound closely together, and because they cannot understand the own-nature of form and the rest, the body of the five consciousnesses turns. Mahamati, together with the five consciousnesses, or by distinguishing the marks of different objects, the mental consciousness arises; yet those consciousnesses do not think, ‘We are simultaneous and serve as each other’s causes,’ but toward the objects appearing in their own minds, discrimination and grasping arise together, each knowing its own object with no mark of difference. Mahamati, when practitioners enter samadhi, through the subtle stirring of habit-power they do not know it, but only think, ‘I have extinguished the consciousnesses and entered samadhi.’ In truth they have not extinguished the consciousnesses and entered samadhi, because the seeds of habit-energy are not extinguished; only by not grasping at objects is it called extinction of consciousness.

“Mahamati, thus the course of the storehouse consciousness is subtle; none but the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas dwelling on the grounds, and not all the rest—the two vehicles, the non-Buddhists, and their powers of concentration and wisdom—can know it. Only a practitioner who practices in accord with reality, who by the power of wisdom understands the marks of the grounds and well penetrates the meaning of the statements, who has gathered roots of goodness in the presence of countless Buddhas, and who does not falsely discriminate what is seen by his own mind, is able to know it. Mahamati, practitioners who dwell in mountain forests and cultivate the upper, middle, and lower, can see the flowing of their own mind’s discrimination, attain the supernormal faculties and the power of mastery in the various samadhis, receive the consecration of the Buddhas and be surrounded by bodhisattvas, know the range of mind, intellect, and consciousness, and cross the great ocean of birth and death with its craving, karma, and ignorance. Therefore you should draw near to Buddhas and bodhisattvas and to good teachers who practice in accord with reality.”
Then the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Like the waves of the mighty ocean, stirred up by a fierce wind,
The surging billows lash the dark abyss and never cease.
The ocean of the storehouse consciousness ever dwells, moved by the wind of objects;
The waves of the various consciousnesses leap up and turn to birth.
Blue, red, and the other colors, salt, shell, milk, and rock-honey,
Flowers, fruits, the sun and moon—neither different nor not different.
The seven consciousnesses, beginning with the intellect, should be known as just the same,
Like the ocean with its waves, arising together with the mind.
Just as the ocean waters stir and the many waves roll on,
So too with the storehouse consciousness: the many consciousnesses arise.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness are spoken of for the sake of characteristics;
The eight consciousnesses have no separate marks, no grasping or grasped.
Like the ocean and its waves, they are without distinction;
So it is with the mind of the various consciousnesses: their difference too is unattainable.
The mind can accumulate karma; the intellect can accumulate it widely;
Because it discerns, it is called consciousness; toward manifest objects it is called the five.”
Then Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva asked in verse:
“The images of blue, red, and other colors appear in the consciousness of beings;
Like waves, the various dharmas—I pray the Buddha will explain.”
Then the World-Honored One answered in verse:
“The images of blue, red, and other colors are unattainable in the waves;
The mind gives rise to the many marks, awakening ordinary beings.
Yet that originally does not arise, apart from what one’s own mind grasps;
Grasping and grasped are the same as those waves.
Body, possessions, and dwelling appear from the consciousness of beings;
Therefore, seeing this arising, it is no different from the waves.”
Then Mahamati spoke again in verse:
“The nature of the great ocean’s waves can be distinguished as they leap;
The storehouse consciousness arises thus—why do you not know it?”
“The alaya is like the ocean, the turning consciousnesses like its waves;
For ordinary beings without wisdom, similes are widely set forth.”
“As when the sunlight rises, it shines equally above and below;
So too the lamp of the world should speak the truth to the foolish.
Since you can already reveal the Dharma, why not make the real clear?”
“If one speaks of the real, that mind has no reality.
Like ocean waves, an image in a mirror, or a dream;
They appear all at once, and so it is with the range of mind.
Because the objects are not complete, they turn to birth in due order;
Consciousness knows by discerning, and the intellect thinks it so as well.
The five consciousnesses know manifest objects, with no fixed order;
Like a master painter and the painter’s apprentices,
Who spread their colors and paint many images, so I say it is as well.
In the colors there is no writing, nor brush, nor yet the silk.
To delight beings, bright and varied images are made;
Speech and words then alter, but the real is apart from letters.
The real Dharma in which I dwell is taught for the sake of practitioners;
In the place of self-realization of the real, grasping and grasped are apart.
This is taught for the sons of the Buddha; for the foolish it is expounded otherwise;
All is like an illusion; what is seen is unattainable.
Thus the various teachings alter according to the matter at hand;
What is spoken may not be fitting, and for that one it is no teaching.
Like the many sick, for whom a good physician gives medicine as fits;
So the Tathagata, for beings, teaches according to mind and measure.
The refuge of the world, the range of realized wisdom—
Not the range of non-Buddhists, nor likewise of the shravakas.

“Furthermore, Mahamati, if a bodhisattva-mahasattva wishes to understand that the discriminated objects of grasping and grasped are all what one’s own mind manifests, they should keep far from commotion, torpor, and sleep, and diligently cultivate throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night; they should keep far from the wrong treatises of non-Buddhists they have heard and from the dharmas of the two vehicles, and thoroughly penetrate the marks of their own mind’s discrimination.

“Furthermore, Mahamati, when a bodhisattva-mahasattva has dwelt in the marks dwelt in by the wisdom-mind, they should diligently cultivate the three marks of supreme noble wisdom. What are the three? They are: the mark of no reflected image, the mark of being upheld by the vows of all Buddhas, and the mark of the range of self-realized noble wisdom. Once practitioners attain these marks, they abandon the mark of the wisdom-mind of a lame donkey and enter the bodhisattva’s eighth ground, cultivating these three marks without letting go. Mahamati, the mark of no reflected image arises through habituating oneself to all the marks of the two vehicles and non-Buddhists; the mark of being upheld by the vows of all Buddhas arises through the sustaining power of the Buddhas’ own original vows; the mark of the range of self-realized noble wisdom arises through not grasping at the marks of any dharma, accomplishing the illusory bodies of the samadhis, and ranging into the wisdom of the Buddha ground. Mahamati, these are called the three marks of supreme noble wisdom. If one attains these marks, one reaches the range of self-realized noble wisdom; you and the bodhisattva-mahasattvas should diligently cultivate them.”

Then Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, and sustained by the majestic power of all the Buddhas, said to the Buddha: “I pray you teach the Dharma-gate of the noble wisdom and own-nature that is the basis of the distinctions among the one hundred and eight statements, by which all Tathagatas, worthy ones, and perfectly enlightened ones, for the sake of bodhisattva-mahasattvas who fall into shared and individual characteristics, teach this gate of the distinctions of the nature of false reckoning; for once this meaning is known, they can purify the field of contemplation of the two selflessnesses and illumine the grounds, transcend the bliss of the samadhis of all the two vehicles and non-Buddhists, see the inconceivable range of action of the Tathagatas, utterly abandon the five dharmas and own-natures, adorn themselves with the wisdom of the dharmakaya of all Buddhas, enter the realm of illusion and dwell in all lands, and in the Tushita palace and the highest heaven of form accomplish the Tathagata body.”

The Buddha said: “Mahamati, there is a kind of non-Buddhist who, seeing that all dharmas come to an end according to causes, gives rise to a discriminating understanding, conceives of the hornless hare and so gives rise to a view of nonexistence: as the hare’s horn is nonexistent, so are all dharmas likewise. There are other non-Buddhists who, having seen that the great elements, the qualities, the dust-motes, and other things each differ in shape, measure, and position, hold to the hare’s hornlessness as nonexistent and on this basis give rise to the notion that the bull has horns. Mahamati, they fall into dualistic views and do not understand mind-only, but only increase discrimination in their own minds. Mahamati, body, livelihood, and the vessel-world and so on—all are only what discrimination manifests. Mahamati, you should know that the hare’s horn is apart from existence and nonexistence; so it is with all dharmas—do not give rise to discrimination. How is the hare’s horn apart from existence and nonexistence? Because they are mutually dependent. Analyzing the bull’s horn down to dust-motes, its essential mark is in the end unattainable; the range of noble wisdom is far from that view, and therefore you should not discriminate about it.”

Then Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, do they not, by a false view, give rise to marks, and by comparing and observing, falsely reckon it as nonexistent?”

The Buddha said: “It is not that by discrimination one gives rise to marks and, depending on these, speaks of nonexistence. Why? Because they take discrimination as the cause of arising and take the discrimination of horns as what it depends on; since what it depends on is the cause, it is neither different nor not different, and it is not by mutual dependence that the hare’s horn is shown to be nonexistent. Mahamati, if this discrimination were different from the hare’s horn, it would not be the cause of the horn; if it were not different, it would arise depending on it. Mahamati, analyzing the bull’s horn down to the finest dust-mote, it is unattainable; to call it nonexistent while it differs from the horned is a discrimination that is decidedly unreasonable. If both are nonexistent, who depends on whom? If mutual dependence is not established, then to say the hare’s horn is nonexistent because it depends on the existent should not be discriminated, since the cause is not valid. Those who speak of existence and nonexistence grasp at existence and grasp at nonexistence; both are not established.

“Mahamati, there are further non-Buddhists who, seeing the shape of form and the boundaries of space, give rise to grasping, and say that form is different from space and so give rise to discrimination. Mahamati, space is form, entering into the category of form. Mahamati, form is space, because of the nature of the supported and the supporting being established; thus should the boundaries of form and space be known. Mahamati, when the great elements arise, their own marks are each distinct, and they do not dwell in space, yet space is not absent from them. Mahamati, so too with the hare’s horn: depending on the bull’s horn, one says that horn is nonexistent. Mahamati, analyzing the bull’s horn down to dust-motes, and analyzing those dust-motes again, their marks do not appear. On what then does it depend that one says it is nonexistent? If it depends on something else, that too would be likewise. Mahamati, you should keep far from all discrimination of the hare’s horn, the bull’s horn, space, and form; you and the bodhisattva-mahasattvas should constantly observe the marks of discrimination seen by your own minds, and in all lands teach the sons of the Buddha the method of cultivating the observation of one’s own mind.”
Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“What the mind sees does not exist; it arises only depending on mind;
Body, possessions, and the shadows of dwelling appear from beings’ storehouse consciousness.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness, own-nature, and the five dharmas,
The purity of the two selflessnesses—these the guides expound.
Long and short are mutually observed and depend on each other;
Because the one exists the other becomes nonexistent; because the one does not exist the other becomes existent.
Analyzing the atom, no form is ever produced;
Mind-only is what is established—the holders of evil views do not believe it.
It is no sphere for the sectarians, nor yet for the hearers;
What the Saviors of the world proclaim is the realm of self-realization.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, for the sake of purifying the flow of what appears in the mind, asked the Buddha: “World-Honored One, how is the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings purified? Is it purified gradually, or is it purified at once?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, it is purified gradually, not at once. As the mango fruit ripens gradually, not at once, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings—gradually, not at once. As a potter shapes his vessels gradually, not at once, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings—gradually, not at once. As the great earth brings forth grasses and trees gradually, not at once, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings—gradually, not at once. Mahāmati, as a person learns music, writing, painting, and all the various arts gradually, not at once, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings—gradually, not at once. But as a bright mirror shows all images at once, without discrimination, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings—showing at once all realms free of marks, and yet without discrimination. As the sun and moon at one time illumine all forms and colors, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the past habits of the mind of all beings—at once revealing to them the inconceivable wisdom-realm of all the Tathāgatas. As the ālaya-consciousness at once reveals the body, the means of living, and the whole realm of the world, so too the Reward Buddha, in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, at once brings all beings to maturity and causes them to cultivate all practices. As the Dharma Buddha at once reveals the Reward Buddha and the Manifestation Buddha, and illumines with light the holy realm of self-realization, so too does he at once reveal the marks of the Dharma and illumine them, causing beings to depart from all evil views of being and non-being.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, as for what flows from the nature of the Dharma: the Buddha teaches the self-marks and common marks of all dharmas, the causal marks of the habit-energy of what appears in the mind, and the causal marks grasped by the imagined nature; mutually bound together, all these phantasms have no self-nature of their own, yet beings grasp them with every kind of attachment and take them as real—all of which can never be obtained.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, attachment to the imagined nature arises depending on the dependent nature. Mahāmati, as a magician, by the power of his illusion, conjures various forms of beings out of grasses, trees, tiles, and stones, and those who see them make all sorts of discriminations, none of them real—so too is this. Mahāmati, by the power of the habit-energy of grasping at realms, within the dependent nature the various marks of the imagined nature appear; this is called the arising of the imagined nature.
