At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, be pleased to tell me of the self-realized nature of the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Awakened, so that I and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas may gain the skill to awaken ourselves and to awaken others.”
The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, as you have asked, so shall I tell you.”

Mahāmati said: “Yes, World-Honored One. Is the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Awakened, made or not made, fruit or cause, mark or what is marked, the spoken or the speaking, the awakened or the awakening, and are such as these different or not different?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Awakened, is neither made nor not made, neither fruit nor cause, neither mark nor what is marked, neither the spoken nor the speaking, neither the awakened nor the awakening. Why? Because both alike are at fault. Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were something made, he would be impermanent; and if impermanent, then all made things would be the Tathāgata, which I and all the Buddhas do not accept. If he were not made, he would have no substance at all, and all the practices one cultivates would be empty and without benefit, like a hare’s horn or the child of a barren woman, since they would not be produced by any making cause. If he were neither cause nor fruit, he would be neither existent nor nonexistent; and if neither existent nor nonexistent, he would transcend the four propositions. The four propositions are spoken only in accord with the world. If one transcends the four propositions, there is only speech, and that is like the child of a barren woman. Mahāmati, the child of a barren woman is only speech and does not fall into the four propositions; because it does not fall into them, it cannot be measured. All who have wisdom should thus know the meaning of all the Tathāgata’s propositions. Mahāmati, when I say that all dharmas are without self, it is because within all dharmas there is no self-nature that I speak of no-self; it is not that all dharmas have no self-nature. The meaning of the Tathāgata’s propositions should be understood in the same way. Mahāmati, just as a cow has not the nature of a horse and a horse has not the nature of a cow, yet neither is without its own nature, so too are all dharmas: they have no self-mark, and yet it is not that they exist or do not exist; this is not something the foolish can know. Why can they not know it? Because of discrimination. That all dharmas are empty, that all dharmas are unborn, that all dharmas have no self-nature—all this is likewise so. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata and the aggregates are neither different nor not different. If they were not different, he would be impermanent, for the five aggregates are made things. If they were different, then it would be like the two horns of a cow, which are different and yet not different: they are not different because they resemble each other, and they are different because they differ in length; thus the right horn of a cow differs from the left and the left from the right, in length and in form and color each is distinct, and yet they are not different. As with the aggregates, so with the elements and sense-fields: all dharmas are likewise so.

“Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is spoken of in dependence on liberation, and the Tathāgata and liberation are neither different nor not different. If they were different, the Tathāgata would be bound up with the marks of form, and being bound up with the marks of form he would be impermanent. If they were not different, then the cultivator’s vision should admit of no distinction; but since there is distinction, they are not not different. So too are wisdom and the known: neither different nor not different. And if neither different nor not different, then they are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither made nor made-things, neither action nor non-action, neither the awakened nor the awakening, neither mark nor what is marked, neither the aggregates nor different from the aggregates, neither the spoken nor the speaking, neither one nor different, neither both nor not both. For this reason they transcend all measure; transcending all measure, there is only speech; there being only speech, there is no arising; there being no arising, there is no ceasing; there being no ceasing, they are like empty space. Mahāmati, space is neither made nor a made-thing; being neither made nor a made-thing, it is far from all conditions; being far from all conditions, it passes beyond all dharmas of conceptual elaboration; and passing beyond all dharmas of conceptual elaboration, it is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is the very essence of the Fully Awakened, and the Fully Awakened is forever free of all the spheres of the senses.”
“Beyond all measures of the senses, neither fruit nor yet cause;
Marks and what is marked and the like—all these he is utterly free of.
The aggregates, conditions, and perfect awakening—none can see them as one or different;
Since there is no seer at all, how could discrimination arise?
Neither made nor not made, neither cause nor not cause,
Neither the aggregates nor not the aggregates, nor yet apart from other things.
There is no single dharma-essence, as their discrimination sees;
Nor yet is it nonexistent—such is the nature of all dharmas.
Depending, non-being becomes being; depending, being becomes non-being;
Since non-being cannot be grasped, being too should not be spoken of.
Not understanding self and no-self, they only cling to language;
They drown in the two extremes, ruining themselves and ruining the world.
If one can see this dharma, one is free of every fault;
This is called right seeing, and one does not revile the Great Teacher.”

At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, it is said in the Buddha’s scriptures that one discriminates and grasps non-arising and non-ceasing, and that this is another name for the Tathāgata. World-Honored One, be pleased to tell me: since this non-arising and non-ceasing is a nothing, how can it be said to be another name for the Tathāgata? As the World-Honored One says that all dharmas are unborn and unceasing, one should know that this falls into the view of being and non-being. World-Honored One, if a dharma is unborn it cannot be grasped; there is not the slightest dharma—who then is the Tathāgata? I pray the World-Honored One to proclaim this for me.”

The Buddha said: “Listen well, and I shall tell you. Mahāmati, what I teach as the Tathāgata is not a nothing, nor does it grasp non-arising and non-ceasing, nor does it await conditions, nor is it without meaning. When I speak of non-arising, this is but another name for the Tathāgata’s mind-made dharmakāya, and all the sectarians, the hearers and solitary realizers, and the Bodhisattvas of the seventh ground do not understand its meaning. Mahāmati, just as Indra, the earth, space, and even hands and feet—each and every thing has many names, yet it is not that because the names are many the substance is many, nor that there is no substance. Mahāmati, so it is with me: in this Sahā world I have three asamkhyeyas of hundreds of thousands of names. Though the foolish hear them and speak them, they do not know them to be other names for the Tathāgata. Among them are those who know the Tathāgata, who know the Teacherless One, who know the Guide, who know the Supreme Guide, who know the Universal Guide, who know him as the Buddha, who know him as the King of Bulls, who know him as Brahmā, who know him as Viṣṇu, who know him as Īśvara, who know him as the Victor, who know him as Kapila, who know him as the Limit of Reality, who know him as the Inexhaustible, who know him as the Auspicious, who know him as Wind, who know him as Fire, who know him as Kubjira, who know him as the Moon, who know him as the Sun, who know him as the King, who know him as the Sage, who know him as Śukra, who know him as Indra, who know him as the Morning Star, who know him as Great Strength, who know him as Water, who know him as the Undying, who know him as the Unborn, who know him as Emptiness of Nature, who know him as Suchness, who know him as Truth, who know him as Reality, who know him as the Limit of Reality, who know him as the Dharma-realm, who know him as Nirvāṇa, who know him as the Ever-abiding, who know him as Equality, who know him as Non-duality, who know him as the Markless, who know him as Peace, who know him as the Possessor of Marks, who know him as Causality, who know him as Buddha-nature, who know him as the Instructor, who know him as Liberation, who know him as the Path, who know him as the Omniscient, who know him as the Supreme, who know him as the Mind-made Body—thus do they fulfill three asamkhyeyas of hundreds of thousands of names, neither increasing nor decreasing. In this world and in other worlds, there are those who can know me as the moon in the water, neither entering nor leaving; but the foolish, their minds sunk in the two extremes, cannot understand, though they revere, serve, and make offerings, and do not rightly understand the meaning of names, words, and phrases. Clinging to the verbal teaching, they are blind to the truth and say that non-arising and non-ceasing is without substance, not knowing it to be the Tathāgata’s distinct names; like those who say Indra, Śakra, and the rest. Taking faith in the verbal teaching, they are blind to the truth, and in regard to all dharmas they take the meaning as the words say. Those foolish people speak thus: the meaning is as the words say, and the meaning and the words are not different. Why? Because the meaning, they say, has no substance. Such a person does not understand the self-nature of sounds and words, and holds that the words are the meaning itself, with no separate meaning-substance. Mahāmati, that person is foolish and does not know that words are born and cease, while the meaning is unborn and unceasing. Mahāmati, all words fall into letters, but the meaning does not fall into them, because it is apart from being and non-being, and because it is unborn and without substance. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata does not teach a dharma that falls into letters, because the existence and nonexistence of letters cannot be grasped—save for those who do not fall into letters. Mahāmati, if a person teaches dharma while falling into letters, his teaching is false and deceitful. Why? Because the self-nature of all dharmas is apart from letters. Therefore, Mahāmati, it is said in my scriptures that I and all the Buddhas and all the Bodhisattvas do not speak a single word and do not answer a single word. Why is that? Because all dharmas are apart from letters, yet it is not that they are not discriminated and taught in accord with the meaning. Mahāmati, if nothing were taught, the teaching would be cut off; and if the teaching were cut off, there would be no hearers, solitary realizers, Bodhisattvas, or Buddhas; and if there were none of these at all, who would teach and for whom? Therefore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should not cling to letters but should teach the dharma according to what is fitting. I and all the Buddhas set it forth in many ways, according to the afflictions, understandings, and desires of beings, so that they may know that all dharmas are what their own minds display and have no outer objects, and may abandon the two discriminations and turn the mind, manas, and consciousness—not in order to establish the holy self-realization.

“Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should follow the meaning and not rely on letters. One who relies on letters falls into evil views, clings to his own school and gives rise to speech; he cannot rightly understand the marks and the words, phrases, and sentences of all dharmas; he ruins himself and ruins others, and cannot cause people to attain understanding. But one who rightly knows the marks of all dharmas, and comprehends all words, phrases, and meanings, can cause himself to receive the joy of the markless and can also cause others to abide in the Great Vehicle. If he can cause others to abide in the Great Vehicle, he is embraced by all Buddhas, hearers, solitary realizers, and Bodhisattvas; if he is embraced by all Buddhas, hearers, solitary realizers, and Bodhisattvas, he can embrace all beings; if he can embrace all beings, he can embrace all right dharmas; if he can embrace all right dharmas, the Buddha-lineage is not cut off; and if the Buddha-lineage is not cut off, he attains a surpassing and wondrous place. Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is born in a surpassing and wondrous place, wishing to cause beings to abide in the Great Vehicle, displays all kinds of forms by the ten powers of sovereignty, and teaches the true dharma according to what is fitting. The true dharma is without difference and without distinction, neither coming nor going, and all conceptual elaborations are utterly stilled. Therefore, Mahāmati, good men and good women should not cling to the meaning according to the words. Why? Because the true dharma is apart from letters.

“Mahāmati, suppose a man points at something with his finger, and a child looks at the finger and does not look at the thing. So too are foolish ordinary people: following the finger of speech, they give rise to clinging, and to the end of their lives they cannot abandon the finger of letters and grasp the supreme meaning. Mahāmati, suppose an infant should eat cooked food, and someone who does not understand the skill of cooking gives him raw food, and he becomes deranged. So too is non-arising and non-ceasing: without the skill of cultivation it becomes unwholesome. Therefore one should well cultivate the skills, and not follow speech as though gazing at the fingertip. Mahāmati, the true meaning is subtle and still, and is the cause of nirvāṇa; speech is joined with vain imagining and turns in birth and death. Mahāmati, the true meaning is gained from much hearing. Much hearing means skill in the meaning, not skill in speech. One who is skilled in the meaning does not follow the evil views of any sectarian, and does not follow them himself and causes others not to follow them; this is called much hearing in the meaning. One who seeks the meaning should draw near to such a one, and one who clings to letters, being the opposite of this, should quickly be left behind.”

At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, the Tathāgata’s teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing is nothing remarkable. Why? The sectarians also say that the maker is unborn and unceasing, and the World-Honored One also says that space, nirvāṇa, and the extinction of the two are unborn and unceasing. The sectarians also say that the maker, by causes and conditions, produces the world; the World-Honored One also says that ignorance, craving, and karma produce all worlds; both are by causes and conditions, only the names differ. So too is it with outer things and their causes and conditions. Therefore the Buddha’s teaching and the sectarians’ teaching are without difference. The sectarians say that the atom, the supreme, the sovereign, the lord of creatures, and so forth, these nine things, are unborn and unceasing; the World-Honored One also says that all dharmas are unborn and unceasing, and that being and non-being alike cannot be grasped. World-Honored One, the great elements do not perish, for their own marks are unborn and unceasing, and they flow through all realms of rebirth without abandoning their own nature. Though the World-Honored One’s distinctions vary somewhat, none of it is other than what the sectarians have already taught; therefore the Buddha-dharma is the same as the sectarians’. If there is any difference, I pray the Buddha to set it forth: for what reason is the Buddha’s teaching superior? If there is no difference, the sectarians are the Buddha, since they too teach non-arising and non-ceasing. The World-Honored One always says that in one world there are not many Buddhas; but by what has just been said, there should be.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the non-arising and non-ceasing that I teach is not the same as the sectarians’ non-arising and non-ceasing, nor their doctrine that the unborn is impermanent. Why? What the sectarians teach is that there is a real nature and mark, unborn and unchanging; I do not fall into the class of being and non-being in that way. The dharma that I teach is neither existent nor nonexistent, apart from arising and apart from ceasing. How is it not nonexistent? Because forms are seen in all kinds of ways, like illusions and dreams. How is it not existent? Because the self-nature of form cannot be grasped, since it is seen and not seen, grasped and not grasped. Therefore I teach that all dharmas are neither existent nor nonexistent. If one awakens to the fact that this is only what one’s own mind displays, and abides in self-nature where discrimination no longer arises, then all the doings of the world are forever stilled; for discrimination is the affair of the foolish, not of the noble. Mahāmati, the deluded mind discriminates unreal objects, like a city of the gandharvas, like a conjured man. Mahāmati, just as a child sees a city of the gandharvas and conjured merchants going in and out, and with a deluded mind discriminates and says there are real things, so too is all that the foolish see, whether arising or not arising, conditioned or unconditioned. As a conjured man arises and a conjured man ceases, yet the conjured man in truth neither arises nor ceases, so too are all dharmas apart from arising and ceasing. Mahāmati, it is the foolish who vainly give rise to the view of arising and ceasing, not the noble ones. To speak of the vain is to give rise to inverted views that do not accord with the dharma-nature. One with inverted views clings to dharmas as having a nature and does not see cessation; and because he does not see cessation, he cannot become free of vain discrimination. Therefore, Mahāmati, the view of the markless is superior, not the view of marks. Marks are the cause of arising; if there are no marks, there is no discrimination, and non-arising and non-ceasing is nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, nirvāṇa means seeing the place of reality, abandoning the discriminations of mind and mental factors, and attaining the Tathāgata’s inner realization of noble wisdom; this I call the nirvāṇa of cessation.”
“To refute the view that things arise, I establish the meaning of non-arising;
I teach the doctrine of no-cause, which the foolish cannot understand.
All dharmas are unborn, and yet are not a nothing;
Like a gandharva city or a dream, they appear though without a cause.
Empty, unborn, without nature—how is this spoken to me?
Apart from all converging conditions, it cannot be seen by wisdom.
Therefore I teach that all is empty, unborn, and without nature;
Each convergence of conditions appears, and yet it has no being.
Analyzed, there is no convergence—not as the sectarians see it;
Like a dream, like falling hairs, a mirage, and a gandharva city.
Arising without a cause and vainly appearing—so are all the affairs of the world;
Subduing the doctrine of a cause, I set forth the purport of non-arising.
If the meaning of non-arising endures, the eye of Dharma is never destroyed;
When I teach the doctrine of no-cause, the sectarians are all terrified.
How, and from what cause? And for what reason do they arise?
Where do they converge, that one should frame a doctrine of no-cause?
Observing conditioned dharmas, they are neither caused nor causeless;
For those who hold to arising and ceasing, their views come to an end right there.
Is it because there is nothing that it does not arise? Or because it awaits conditions?
Is it a name without meaning? Be pleased to tell me.
It is not that being nothing it does not arise, nor that it arises awaiting conditions;
Nor is there a thing that is named, nor a name without meaning.
All the sectarians, the hearers, and the solitary realizers,
Cannot tread the ten abodes—this is the mark of non-arising.
Apart from all causes and conditions, there is no maker at all;
Established by mind alone—this I call non-arising.
Dharmas do not arise from causes, nor are they nonexistent nor existent;
Grasper and grasped, discrimination, are abandoned—this I call non-arising.
When mind alone sees nothing, and is apart from the two natures,
And thus the ground is turned—this I call non-arising.
Outer things exist and do not exist, and the mind grasps nothing of them;
All views are wholly cut off—this is the mark of non-arising.
Emptiness, non-nature, and the like—their meaning is just the same as this;
It is not that being empty it is empty; because it is unborn, emptiness is spoken of.
When causes and conditions gather together, arising and ceasing then come to be;
When causes and conditions are dispersed, arising and ceasing are no more.
If one is apart from all causes and conditions, then there is no dharma at all;
Oneness of nature and difference of nature—these the foolish discriminate.
Being and non-being do not give rise to dharmas, and neither does both;
It is only when conditions converge that arising and ceasing are seen therein.
Following the world, one speaks provisionally of the linked chain of causes and conditions;
If one is apart from the chain of causes and conditions, the meaning of arising cannot be had.
I teach only the linked chain; since there is no arising, there is no non-arising;
Apart from the faults of all sectarians, this the foolish cannot understand.
If, apart from the chain of conditions, there were a dharma that arises;
That would be the doctrine of no-cause, destroying the meaning of the linked chain.
As a lamp can illumine things, so the linked chain appears;
But then, apart from the linked chain, there would be separate dharmas.
Where there is non-arising there is no nature; the essence and mark are like empty space;
Seeking dharmas apart from the linked chain is what foolish men discriminate.
There is also another non-arising, the dharma attained by all the noble ones;
He who is born into that non-arising has the acceptance of non-arising.
All the worlds without exception are nothing but the linked chain;
If one can understand it thus, this person’s mind attains stability.
Ignorance, craving, and karma—these are the inner linked chain;
Seed, clay, wheel, and the like—these are called the outer.
If one says there is some other dharma that arises from causes and conditions,
That is apart from the meaning of the linked chain, and so is not the teaching.
If the arising dharma is not, whose cause and condition is it?
Arising in turn from one another—this is the meaning of causes and conditions.
Solidity, moisture, warmth, motion, and the like—these the foolish discriminate;
Since conditions are without any dharma, non-self-nature is therefore spoken of.
As a physician treats all kinds of illness, his doctrine is without difference;
But because the illnesses differ, the remedies are of many kinds.
For the sake of all beings, I put an end to the illness of afflictions;
Knowing whether their faculties are keen or dull, I set forth all the dharma-gates.
It is not that because afflictions and faculties differ there are all kinds of dharmas;
There is only one Great Vehicle, the cool eightfold path.”

At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, all the sectarians vainly speak of impermanence, and the World-Honored One also says that all formations are impermanent and are dharmas of arising and ceasing. I do not know whether this teaching is false or true. And how many kinds of impermanence are there?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the sectarians say there are seven kinds of impermanence, which are not my dharma. What are the seven? They are these: some say that what is abandoned as soon as it is made is called impermanence, because once born it is not born again, being of the nature of impermanence; some say that the alteration of shape and place is called impermanence; some say that form itself is impermanence; some say that the transformation of form is called impermanence—all dharmas continue without interruption, and this transformation causes them naturally to return to destruction, as milk and curds transform one into the other; though it cannot be seen, yet it is present in dharmas and destroys all dharmas; some say the impermanence of things; some say the impermanence of things and no-things; some say the impermanence of the unborn, which pervades and abides in all dharmas. Among these, the impermanence of things and no-things means that the marks of the made and the maker are destroyed, and the nature of the great elements is from the first without arising. The impermanence of the unborn means that permanence and impermanence, being and non-being, and all such dharmas are without any arising at all; even analyzed down to the atom, nothing is seen; and because there is no arising, it is called unborn. This is the mark of the impermanence of the unborn; one who does not understand it falls into the sectarians’ meaning of the impermanence of arising. As for the meaning of the impermanence of things and the impermanence of things: in the place of the neither permanent nor impermanent, they give rise to their own discrimination. What does this mean? They posit an impermanence that does not itself perish but can destroy all dharmas; for if there were no impermanence to destroy all dharmas, dharmas would never perish and would become nothing. It is as a staff or a stone that can break things while itself not breaking; so too is this. Mahāmati, we plainly see that impermanence and all dharmas have no difference of maker and made; since this is impermanence and this is the made, and there is no difference, maker and made should both be permanent, and no cause is seen that can make dharmas become nothing. Mahāmati, the destruction of dharmas truly does have a cause, but it is not something the foolish can understand.

“Mahāmati, a different cause should not give rise to a different fruit. If it could give rise, all different dharmas would give rise to one another, and between that dharma and this, the producer and the produced, there would be no distinction. Yet we plainly see distinction: how then can a different cause give rise to a different fruit? Mahāmati, if the nature of impermanence were an existing dharma, it would be like made things and would itself be impermanent; and being itself impermanent, the dharmas it makes impermanent should all be permanent. Mahāmati, if the nature of impermanence dwelt in all dharmas, it would be like all dharmas and fall into the three times: with past form it would already have ceased at the same time, future form would not arise, and present form would perish along with it. All the sectarians hold that the substance of the four great elements does not perish, and that form is but the great elements’ differentiated made form; being neither different nor not different, its own nature likewise does not perish. Mahāmati, within the three realms of existence, are not the made and the maker all marks of arising, dwelling, and ceasing? How could there be yet another nature of impermanence that can produce things without itself perishing? As for the impermanence of abandoning as soon as made, it is not that the great elements make one another, for they are each distinct; nor that they make their own marks, for they are not different; nor that they make them together, for they are separate. One should know that this is not the impermanence of the beginning of making. As for the impermanence of the alteration of shape, this is not the destruction of the maker and the made, but only the destruction of shape. What does this mean? It means that when form is analyzed down to the atom, only the sight of shape, length, and the like is destroyed; the substance of the made and the maker is not destroyed. This view falls within the Sāṃkhya. As for form itself being impermanence, this is the impermanence of shape, not the nature of the great elements. If the nature of the great elements were also impermanent, there would be no worldly affairs at all; and one who holds that there are no worldly affairs falls into the view of the Lokāyatas, since he sees that the own marks of all dharmas arise and are only words. As for the impermanence of transformation, it is the substance of form that changes, not the great elements; as when gold is made into ornaments, the ornaments change but the gold does not, so too is this.

“Mahāmati, all such sectarians vainly discriminate and see a nature of impermanence, and they speak thus: fire cannot burn the own marks of fire, but only disperses each of them; if it could burn them, then the maker and the made would be utterly destroyed. Mahāmati, I teach that all dharmas are neither permanent nor impermanent. Why? Because I do not grasp outer dharmas; because the three realms are mind only; because I do not speak of marks; because the nature and the abode of the great elements, with all their differences, are unborn and unceasing; because there is no maker or made; because the two substances of the grasping and the grasped all arise from discrimination; because one knows the nature of the two graspings as it really is; because one understands that they are only what one’s own mind displays; because one is free of the two views of outer being and non-being; and because, free of the views of being and non-being, one does not discriminate maker and made. Mahāmati, the dharmas of the world, of the supramundane, and of the supramundane-supreme are only one’s own mind, neither permanent nor impermanent; those who cannot understand this fall into the sectarians’ evil views of the two extremes. Mahāmati, all the sectarians cannot understand these three kinds of dharma, and relying on their own discrimination they give rise to speech and speak of a nature of impermanence. Mahāmati, the spheres of language and discrimination belonging to these three kinds of dharma are not something the foolish can know.”
“Abandoned as soon as made, shape undergoing change;
Form and things and the like as impermanent—the sectarians vainly discriminate.
Dharmas are without destruction, and the great elements abide in their own nature;
The various views of the sectarians thus speak of impermanence.
All those multitudes of sectarians speak of non-arising and non-ceasing;
If the nature of the great elements is inherently permanent, what dharma is impermanent?
Grasping and the grasped are all only mind;
The two kinds appear from the mind, and there is no self or mine.
Brahmā and all such dharmas—I teach that they are only mind;
If one is apart from the mind, none of them can be had.”

At that time Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, be pleased to tell me of the successive marks of the entry into extinction of all hearers and solitary realizers, so that I and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, rightly knowing this, may have no confusion of mind in the joy of the absorption of extinction, and may not fall into the errors of the two vehicles and of all the sectarians.”
The Buddha said: “Listen well, and I shall tell you.

“Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva reaches the sixth ground, and the hearers and solitary realizers enter the absorption of extinction; the Bodhisattva of the seventh ground enters it in every thought and moment, being apart from the self-nature and marks of all dharmas—which is not the case for the two vehicles. The two vehicles have doings and fall into the grasped and the grasping, and do not attain the mark of the sameness of all dharmas; understanding the own marks and shared marks of the wholesome and the unwholesome, they enter the absorption of extinction, and therefore cannot enter it in every thought and moment. Mahāmati, for the Bodhisattvas of the eighth ground and for the hearers and solitary realizers, the discriminations of thought of mind, manas, and consciousness cease. From the first ground up to the sixth, they observe that all the three realms are only what mind, manas, and consciousness discriminate of themselves, and are apart from self and mine, and they do not see the various marks of outer dharmas. The foolish do not know that, through the defiled habitual energies of beginningless time, within their own minds they turn into marks of the grasped and the grasping and give rise to clinging. Mahāmati, the samādhi attained by the Bodhisattva of the eighth ground is the same as the nirvāṇa of the hearers and solitary realizers; but because he is empowered by the power of all the Buddhas, he does not enter nirvāṇa at the gate of samādhi. If he were not sustained, he would not bring all beings to liberation and could not fulfill the Tathāgata’s ground, and the Tathāgata-lineage would be cut off. Therefore all the Buddhas tell him of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and great virtues, so that he may in the end not enter nirvāṇa. The hearers and solitary realizers cling to the joy of samādhi, and therefore give rise within it to the thought of nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva of the seventh ground can well observe mind, manas, and consciousness, the clinging to self and mine, and the non-self of dharmas, and the own marks and shared marks of the arising and ceasing of dharmas; he is well skilled and decisive in the four unhindered eloquence, and gains mastery at the gate of samādhi, gradually entering all the grounds and fulfilling the factors of bodhi. Mahāmati, it is because I fear that Bodhisattvas may not well understand own marks and shared marks, and may not know the successive order of the grounds, and may fall into the sectarians’ evil views, that I speak thus. Mahāmati, in truth there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor the succession of the grounds, nor coming and going within the three realms; all is only what one’s own mind displays. But the foolish cannot understand this; and because they do not understand, I and all the Buddhas speak thus.

“Mahāmati, when the hearers and solitary realizers reach the eighth ground of the Bodhisattva, they are intoxicated and drunk with the joy of samādhi; they cannot well understand that it is only what the mind displays, and the habitual energies of own marks and shared marks entangle and cover their minds; clinging to the two kinds of non-self, they give rise to the notion of nirvāṇa, which is not the wisdom of cessation. Mahāmati, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees the gate of the joy of the samādhi of cessation, he at once recollects his original vow and great compassion, and fully cultivates the ten inexhaustible phrases; therefore he does not at once enter nirvāṇa—because entering nirvāṇa produces no fruit, because he is apart from the grasped and the grasping, because he understands that it is mind only, because he does not discriminate any dharma, and because he does not fall into the clinging to mind, manas, consciousness, and the nature and marks of outer dharmas. Yet it is not that he does not rouse the right cause of the Buddha-dharma, for he rouses it in accord with the course of wisdom, and thereby attains the Tathāgata’s ground of self-realization. Mahāmati, it is like a man who in a dream crosses a river by skillful means and awakens before crossing; having awakened, he reflects on what he saw before: was it real or was it false? And he thinks to himself: ‘It was neither real nor false; it was only what was seen, heard, perceived, and known—the habitual energies of discrimination of things once experienced—and it appeared in a dream apart from the thought of being and non-being, within consciousness.’ Mahāmati, so too is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: from the first ground up to the seventh, and advancing further into the eighth, he attains non-discrimination, sees all dharmas as illusions and dreams and the like, apart from the grasped and the grasping, sees the vast power and function of mind and mental factors, diligently cultivates the Buddha-dharma and causes what is unattained to be attained, and, apart from the vain discriminations of mind, manas, and consciousness, attains the acceptance of non-arising. This is the nirvāṇa attained by the Bodhisattva; it is not destruction. Mahāmati, in the supreme meaning there is neither succession nor continuity, and it is far from all discrimination of objects; this is what is called the dharma of cessation.”
“The abodes and the Buddha-ground are mind only, without images;
This is what all the Buddhas of past, future, and present have taught.
The seventh ground still has mind; the eighth has no images;
In these two grounds he is said to abide; the rest is what I have attained.
Self-realized and pure — this is my own ground;
In Maheshvara’s supreme abode, adorned as Akaniṣṭha.
Like a great mass of fire, whose flames blaze brightly forth;
It manifests within the three realms, delightful and yet cool.
Some appear as transformations, some were transformed long before;
There it teaches all the vehicles — all are the Tathāgata’s ground.
The ten grounds are the first, the first is the eighth;
The ninth is the seventh, the seventh again the eighth.
The second is the third, the fourth is the fifth;
The third is the sixth — in the signless, what sequence can there be?”

blocks.text: Chapter Five: The Tathāgata, Permanent and Impermanent

inline.s: Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again spoke to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Awakened One, permanent or impermanent?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Awakened One, is neither permanent nor impermanent. Why? Because both views are at fault. How are they at fault? Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were permanent, there would be the fault of a creator, for all non-Buddhists say that the creator is permanent. If he were impermanent, there would be the fault of being something made: he would be like the aggregates, marked by marks, and would at last be annihilated and become nonexistent. Yet the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is in truth not annihilated. Mahāmati, all things made, such as the pot and the cloth, are impermanent; then the Tathāgata would bear the fault of impermanence, and the merit and wisdom he has cultivated would all be empty and without benefit. Moreover, all things made would have to be the Tathāgata, since there is no other cause. Therefore the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent. Again, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is not permanent: were he permanent, he would be like space, which does not await causes to come to be. Mahāmati, for example, space is neither permanent nor impermanent. Why? Because it is free from the faults of permanence and impermanence, of sameness and difference, of both and neither. Again, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is not permanent: were he permanent, he would be unborn, like the horns of a rabbit, a horse, a fish, or a snake.

“Again, Mahāmati, by another meaning he may also be called permanent. Why? Because with present wisdom one realizes the dharma of permanence: the realizing wisdom is permanent, and the Tathāgata is permanent too. Mahāmati, the dharma-nature realized by all Buddhas, the abiding of dharma, the station of dharma, abides unchanging whether the Tathāgata appears in the world or not. It is present in all the dharmas attained by the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists; it is not a mere nothingness, yet it is not something the foolish and unenlightened can know. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is so named because with pure wisdom he inwardly realizes the dharma-nature; he is not named from mind, intellect, or consciousness, nor from the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, which are the habits of false imagination. All the three realms arise from false discrimination; the Tathāgata does not arise from false discrimination. Mahāmati, if anyone holds permanence or impermanence with regard to the twofold, the Tathāgata is without the twofold, for he realizes that all dharmas are without the mark of arising. Therefore he is neither permanent nor impermanent. Mahāmati, as long as there is even the least arising of verbal discrimination, there is the fault of permanence and impermanence. Therefore you should put away the awareness of the two discriminations and not let it remain in the least.”
“Freed from permanence and from impermanence,
Yet manifesting both permanence and impermanence;
Thus one constantly beholds the Buddha, and gives rise to no wrong views.
If one holds to permanence or impermanence, all that is gathered is without benefit;
To put an end to the awareness of discrimination, permanence and impermanence are not taught.
As long as there is any assertion at all, all is confusion;

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again spoke to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I pray you, tell me the marks of the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. If there is no self, who is born and who ceases? Yet ordinary people, relying on arising and ceasing, do not seek the ending of suffering and do not realize nirvāṇa.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, listen well, listen well, and I will tell you. Mahāmati, the tathāgatagarbha is the cause of good and of evil, and can bring forth and produce all destinies and births. Like a magician it manifests all destinies, free from self and what belongs to self; but because of not awakening, when the three conditions come together, a fruit is born. Non-Buddhists do not know this and cling to it as a creator. Perfumed by beginningless habits of falsity and evil, it is called the ālaya-consciousness, and it gives rise to the seven consciousnesses on the ground of ignorance, like the great ocean giving rise to waves, its substance continuing without interruption, forever flowing on. Its own nature is pure, beyond the fault of impermanence, beyond the doctrine of a self. The remaining seven consciousnesses — mind, intellect, and the rest — arise and cease moment by moment; false imagination is their cause, and the marks of objects their condition, and when these come together they are born. Not understanding that form and the rest are what one’s own mind manifests, they cling to names and marks and give rise to feelings of suffering and pleasure. Bound by names and marks, from craving they are born and again give rise to craving. But when the cause and its conditions, and all the faculties of grasping, cease and do not continue to arise, then one who by his own wisdom discriminates the feelings of suffering and pleasure — whether he attains the absorption of cessation, or the four dhyānas, or enters well into the liberation of the truths — falsely gives rise to the thought that he has attained liberation, though in truth he has not abandoned or transformed the name of ālaya-consciousness within the tathāgatagarbha. If there were no ālaya-consciousness, the seven consciousnesses would cease. Why? Because they arise from it as their cause and from conditions. Yet this is not a realm known to any of the non-Buddhists or the two vehicles in their practice, for they know only the nature of the selflessness of persons, and they grasp the particular and shared marks of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. But when one sees the tathāgatagarbha, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the selflessness of all dharmas, then according to the stages one gradually transforms and ceases them; one is no longer moved by the wrong views of non-Buddhists, dwells on the ground of immovability, and attains the ten kinds of gates of the bliss of samādhi. Sustained by the Buddhas through the power of samādhi, one contemplates the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas and the power of original vows, does not dwell in the ultimate reality or in the bliss of samādhi, and attains the wisdom of self-realization, which is not shared by the two vehicles or the non-Buddhists, and wins the path of the ten noble lineages and the mind-born body of wisdom, beyond all conditioned activities. Therefore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who wishes to attain the supreme dharma should purify the name of the tathāgatagarbha, the ālaya-consciousness. Mahāmati, if there were no tathāgatagarbha named ālaya-consciousness, there would be no arising and ceasing. Yet ordinary people and the noble ones alike all have arising and ceasing. Therefore all who practice, though they see the inner realm and dwell in the bliss of the present dharma, do not abandon their courageous and strenuous effort. Mahāmati, this tathāgatagarbha, the ālaya-consciousness, is by nature pure, but is stained by adventitious defilements and so becomes impure. All the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists, by conjecture and opinion, cannot realize it directly; but the Tathāgata sees it clearly and distinctly, as one sees an āmalaka fruit in the palm of the hand.

“Mahāmati, it was for Queen Śrīmālā and for the other bodhisattvas of profound and wondrous pure wisdom that I taught the tathāgatagarbha named ālaya-consciousness, arising together with the seven consciousnesses, so that the hearers might see the selflessness of dharmas. Mahāmati, it was for Queen Śrīmālā that I taught the realm of the Buddha, which is not the realm of non-Buddhists or of the two vehicles. Mahāmati, this tathāgatagarbha, the ālaya-consciousness, is the realm of the Buddha, the place walked by you and the other bodhisattvas of pure wisdom who accord with the meaning; it is not the place walked by any who cling to words, whether non-Buddhists or the two vehicles. Therefore you and all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should diligently contemplate the tathāgatagarbha, the ālaya-consciousness, and not think it enough merely to have heard of it.”
“The tathāgatagarbha, profound and deep, together with the seven consciousnesses;
Clinging gives rise to two kinds of birth; knowing this, one is far removed.
Perfumed by habits without beginning, it appears in the mind like an image;
If one can contemplate it as it truly is, the marks of objects are all nonexistent.
As the fool looks at the finger when shown the moon, watching the finger and not the moon;
So one who clings to words does not see my true reality.
The mind is like a magician, the intellect like his assistant;
The five consciousnesses are the companions, false imagination the audience watching the show.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again spoke to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I pray you tell me the marks of the difference between the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the selflessness of the various consciousnesses. When I and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have understood this well, we shall gradually cultivate the grounds and fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, and reach the Tathāgata’s own realization.”

The Buddha said: “Listen well, and I will tell you. Mahāmati, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the selflessness of the various consciousnesses are these: name, mark, discrimination, right knowledge, and suchness. If a practitioner contemplates these dharmas, he enters the Tathāgata’s own realization, is far removed from the views of permanence and annihilation, of being and nonbeing, and attains the bliss of the present dharma and a profound samādhi. Mahāmati, the foolish do not understand the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the selflessness of the various consciousnesses; seeing external things in what their own minds manifest, they give rise to discrimination — which the noble ones do not do.”
Mahāmati said: “How is it that not understanding, they give rise to discrimination?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the foolish do not know that name is falsely posited. Their minds flow along with it and see all kinds of marks; they reckon a self and what belongs to a self, are defiled by attachment to form, obscure the noble wisdom, give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion, and perform all kinds of karma, like a silkworm making its cocoon. Wrapped about by their own false imagination, they fall into the great ocean of birth and death within the destinies, circling without cease like a water-wheel. They do not know that all dharmas are like an illusion, like a flame, like a moon in the water; what their own minds see is produced by false discrimination. Apart from the grasped and the grasper, apart from arising, abiding, and ceasing, they say these arise from Ishvara, from time, from atoms, or from primal nature, and they flow along with names and marks. Mahāmati, among these, ‘mark’ means this: what the eye-consciousness sees is called form; what the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness receive is called sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharma. These and the like I call marks. ‘Discrimination’ means setting up all manner of names to display the marks — as when by the names of elephant, horse, chariot, foot-soldier, man, woman, and so on their marks are shown, and one decides that this matter is thus and not otherwise. This is called discrimination. ‘Right knowledge’ means contemplating that names and marks are each other’s guests, that the discriminating mind does not arise, that one does not fall into permanence or annihilation, and does not fall into the grounds of non-Buddhists or of the two vehicles. This is called right knowledge. Mahāmati, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva with right knowledge contemplates names and marks, they are neither existent nor nonexistent; he is far from the wrong views of the two extremes of loss and gain, and names, marks, and consciousness are from the first not arisen. This dharma I call suchness.

“Mahāmati, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in suchness, he attains the non-illumined manifest realm, rises to the Ground of Joy, is far from the evil destinies of non-Buddhists, enters the supramundane dharma, ripens in the marks of dharma, knows all dharmas to be like an illusion, realizes the dharma walked by his own noble wisdom, is free from conjectural views, and so passes in order even to the Dharma Cloud. Having reached the Dharma Cloud, with the powers of samādhi, the superknowledges, and sovereign mastery, he opens and fulfills and becomes the Tathāgata. Having become the Tathāgata, for the sake of beings he manifests his body everywhere like a moon in the water, and teaches the dharma according to their wishes and delights. His body is pure, beyond mind, intellect, and consciousness; clad in the armor of the great vow, he fully accomplishes the ten inexhaustible vows. This is what a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva obtains by entering suchness.”
Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again spoke to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, do the three natures enter into the five dharmas, or does each have its own mark?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness all enter into the five dharmas. Among them, name and mark are the nature of false reckoning. Because the discriminated dharmas of mind and mental factors arise together depending on them, they are the nature of dependent origination, like the sun and its light. Right knowledge and suchness are indestructible, and so are the perfected nature. Mahāmati, when attachment arises toward what one’s own mind manifests, eight kinds of discrimination arise; these marks of difference are all unreal, and are only the nature of false reckoning. If one can abandon the two kinds of clinging to self, the wisdom of the two selflessnesses grows. Mahāmati, the stages of the noble wisdom of self-realization of hearers, solitary realizers, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas, and all Buddha-dharmas, are all gathered into these five dharmas. Again, Mahāmati, the five dharmas are these: mark, name, discrimination, suchness, and right knowledge. Among them, ‘mark’ means the shapes of what is seen, such as form, each distinct — this is called mark. Depending on those marks one sets up names such as ‘pot,’ and this is thus and not otherwise — this is called name. Setting up all manner of names to display the marks to mind and mental factors is called discrimination. Those names and those marks are in the end nonexistent; they are only the false mind discriminating over and over. To contemplate thus, even to the ceasing of awareness, is called suchness. Mahāmati, the true, decisive, ultimate, fundamental self-nature that can be attained is the mark of suchness. I and all the Buddhas have realized and entered it in accord, and proclaim and teach it according to its true marks. If one can accord with it and understand it, is free from annihilation and permanence, gives rise to no discrimination, and enters the place of self-realization, going beyond the realm of non-Buddhists and the two vehicles — this is called right knowledge. Mahāmati, these five dharmas gather up completely the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, the two selflessnesses, and all Buddha-dharmas. Mahāmati, in this dharma you should with your own wisdom become skillful and penetrating, and also encourage others to penetrate it. Having penetrated it, the mind is then decisive and does not follow others.”
“The five dharmas and the three self-natures, together with the eight kinds of consciousness;
The two kinds of selflessness — all are gathered into the Mahāyāna.
Name, mark, and discrimination are held by the two self-natures;
Right knowledge and suchness — these are the mark of perfection.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again spoke to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, the scriptures say that the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. How should this be taken? Should it be accepted literally, or does it have another meaning?”

The Buddha told Mahāmati: “Do not accept it literally. Mahāmati, the Buddhas of the three times are not like the sands of the Ganges. Why? The Tathāgata is supreme, surpassing all the world; there is none equal to him, and no simile can reach him. Only a small part of him is used as a simile. Because ordinary people and non-Buddhists constantly cling in their minds to permanence and impermanence, their wrong views grow and they revolve in birth and death. To turn them toward disgust and detachment and to arouse in them a noble longing, I say that the Buddha is easily accomplished and easily met. If I said he is as hard to meet as the udumbara flower, they would lose heart and not strive diligently. Therefore I say he is like the sands of the Ganges. And again, at times, observing those to be taught, I say the Buddha is hard to meet, like the udumbara flower. Mahāmati, the udumbara flower has never been seen, is not seen, and will not be seen; but the Tathāgata has been seen and will be seen. Mahāmati, such similes do not speak of his own dharma. His own dharma is the realm walked by inward noble wisdom; it has no equal in the world and surpasses all similes, and all ordinary people and fools cannot believe or accept it. Mahāmati, the true Tathāgata surpasses the marks seen by mind, intellect, and consciousness; no simile can be set up within it. Yet at times one is set up for their sake, saying ‘like the sands of the Ganges,’ and there is no contradiction. Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges are trodden by turtles, fish, elephants, and horses, yet give rise to no discrimination and remain forever pure and undefiled — so the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom is like that river, and the powers, superknowledges, and sovereign mastery are its sands. Non-Buddhists, like turtles and fish, strive to disturb them, yet the Buddha gives rise to not one thought of discrimination. Why? Because of the Tathāgata’s original vow, to bring peace to all beings with the bliss of samādhi, and because, like the sands of the Ganges, he has no love, no hatred, and no discrimination. Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges are the earth’s own nature, and when the kalpa is consumed by fire and all the earth is burned, the earth element does not abandon its own nature, because it is forever born together with the fire element — and ordinary people say the earth is burned, though in truth it is not burned, for fire is its cause — so too the Tathāgata’s dharma-body is like the sands of the Ganges and is never destroyed. Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges have no limit, so the Tathāgata’s radiance is likewise, for the sake of maturing countless beings, shining upon all the assemblies of all the Buddhas. Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges abide in the nature of sand and do not change into anything else, so too the Tathāgata does not arise or cease in the world, because all causes of birth have been cut off. Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges are not seen to lessen when taken nor to increase when given, so too the Buddhas neither lessen nor increase as they mature beings by the wisdom of skillful means. Why? Because the Tathāgata’s dharma-body has no body. Mahāmati, because there is a body, there is destruction; because the dharma-body has no body, it has no destruction. Mahāmati, just as from the sands of the Ganges, though they be pressed and worked, one seeks in vain for sesamum oil — so too the Tathāgata, though pressed by the many sufferings of beings, and though even the crawling creatures have not yet entered nirvāṇa, if one would have him abandon his profound wish and joy within the dharma-realm, it cannot be found. Why? Because he has fully accomplished the mind of great compassion. Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges flow along with the water and are never without water, so too all the dharma the Tathāgata teaches follows the stream of nirvāṇa. Therefore it is said that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are like the sands of the Ganges. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s teaching does not follow destiny, for destiny means destruction; the ultimate beginning of birth and death cannot be known, and since it cannot be known, how can one speak of destiny? Mahāmati, the meaning of destiny is cessation, which the foolish do not know.”
Mahāmati the Bodhisattva again spoke to the Buddha: “If the ultimate beginning of birth and death cannot be known, how do beings in birth and death attain liberation?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, when the cause of the beginningless habits of falsity and fault is extinguished, and one understands that outer objects are what one’s own mind manifests, the transformation of the basis of discrimination is called liberation. It is not annihilation; therefore one cannot say it has no limit. Mahāmati, ‘without limit’ is only another name for discrimination. Mahāmati, apart from the discriminating mind there is no other being. When one contemplates all dharmas within and without with wisdom, one knows that the knower and the known are both quiescent. Mahāmati, all dharmas are only what one’s own mind discriminates and sees; because one does not understand this, the discriminating mind arises, and when the mind is understood, it ceases.”
“Contemplate all the guides, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
Neither destroyed nor a destiny — such a one can see the Buddha.
Like the sands of the Ganges, utterly free from all faults;
Yet forever flowing in accord — the Buddha’s being is likewise.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again spoke to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I pray you tell me the marks of the momentary destruction of all dharmas. What dharmas are said to be momentary?”

The Buddha said: “Listen well, and I will tell you. Mahāmati, all dharmas are these: good dharmas and bad dharmas, conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas, worldly dharmas and supramundane dharmas, tainted dharmas and untainted dharmas, dharmas with outflows and dharmas without outflows. Mahāmati, to speak briefly, the dharmas of the five aggregates of grasping grow from the cause of the habit-energy of mind, intellect, and consciousness, and the foolish give rise to discrimination toward them, calling them good or bad. The noble ones’ direct realization and dwelling in the bliss of samādhi — this is called the good and untainted dharma. Again, Mahāmati, the good and the bad are the eight consciousnesses. Which are the eight? The tathāgatagarbha, named ālaya-consciousness, together with mind, intellect, and the five consciousnesses. Mahāmati, those five consciousnesses, together with the intellect, produce marks of good and bad, differ from one another, and continue without interruption; born without a distinct substance, they cease as soon as born. Not understanding that objects are what one’s own mind manifests, when they cease in succession another consciousness arises; the intellect, together with those five consciousnesses, grasps all manner of distinct shapes and marks, and does not abide for a moment. These I call momentary dharmas. Mahāmati, the tathāgatagarbha named ālaya-consciousness, together with the intellect and the rest and all the habit-energies, is a momentary dharma; the untainted habit-energy is not a momentary dharma, and this the foolish who hold the doctrine of momentariness cannot know. Because they cannot know that all dharmas are in this way momentary and not momentary, they reckon the unconditioned to be like the destruction of all dharmas and fall into the view of annihilation. Mahāmati, the five consciousnesses do not flow on and do not receive suffering and pleasure, nor are they a cause of nirvāṇa; the tathāgatagarbha receives suffering and pleasure and, together with its causes, has arising and ceasing. Covered over by the four kinds of habit-energy, the foolish, their minds perfumed by discrimination, cannot understand this and give rise to the view of momentariness. Mahāmati, like gold, like a diamond, like the relics of the Buddha, which are of a wondrous nature and are never destroyed: if the dharma that is realized were momentary, then the noble ones would not be noble; yet those noble ones have never been other than noble, like gold and diamonds which, though they remain for a kalpa, do not lessen when weighed. How is it that the foolish do not understand my secret teaching and conceive all dharmas as momentary?”

Mahāmati the Bodhisattva again spoke to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, you always speak of the six pāramitās, and say that when they are fulfilled one attains perfect awakening. Which are the six? How are they fulfilled?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the pāramitās are of three kinds: worldly, supramundane, and supramundane supreme. Mahāmati, the worldly pāramitās are practiced by ordinary people who cling to a self and what belongs to a self, grasp the two extremes, seek the various bodies of existence, and crave form and other objects; practicing thus the pāramitā of giving, of morality, of patience, of effort, and of meditation, they accomplish superknowledges and are born in the Brahma world. Mahāmati, the supramundane pāramitās are practiced by hearers and solitary realizers who cling to nirvāṇa and seek their own bliss, and thus cultivate the pāramitās. Mahāmati, the supramundane supreme pāramitās are practiced by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, as to the two dharmas of his own mind, understands that they are only what discrimination manifests, gives rise to no false imagination, does not produce attachment, does not grasp the marks of form, and for the sake of benefiting and gladdening all beings constantly practices the pāramitā of giving. Giving rise to no discrimination toward any object, he practices the pāramitā of morality. Just when he gives rise to no discrimination, he patiently knows the self-nature of the grasper and the grasped — this is called the pāramitā of patience. Through the first, middle, and last watches of the night he practices diligently without slacking, accords with true understanding, and gives rise to no discrimination — this is called the pāramitā of effort. Giving rise to no discrimination and not giving rise to the non-Buddhist view of nirvāṇa — this is called the pāramitā of meditation. With wisdom he contemplates that the mind is without discrimination, does not fall into the two extremes, transforms and purifies the basis without destroying it, and attains the realm of the noble wisdom of inner realization — this is called the pāramitā of prajñā.”
“The fool discriminates the conditioned as empty, impermanent, and momentary,
Discriminating the meaning of momentariness, like a river, a lamp, a seed.
All dharmas do not arise, are quiescent and without activity;
All things are free of their nature — this is my meaning of momentariness.
Born, it ceases without interval — this is not taught to the foolish;
The uninterruptedly continuing dharmas give rise to discrimination among the destinies.
Ignorance is their cause, and from that the mind is born;
Not yet understanding the coming of form, where in between could it abide?
The uninterrupted continuum ceases, and yet another mind arises;
When it does not abide in form, depending on what does it arise?
If it arises depending on that, its cause is then false;
The cause being false, its substance is not established — how then can it cease each moment?
The practitioner’s absorption, the diamond and the Buddha’s relics;
And the palace of Light-Sound — these the world cannot destroy.
The Tathāgata’s perfect wisdom, and what the monks realize;
The nature of all dharmas constantly abides — how can one see it as momentary?
Forms of the phantom city and illusions — why are they not momentary?
The great elements have no real nature — how can they be said to create?”
The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Five
Taishō Shinshū Daizōkyō, Volume 16, No. 0672, the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra
The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Six

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again spoke to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, why does the Tathāgata bestow upon the arhats the prediction of anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi? Why does he also say that beings without the nature of nirvāṇa shall attain the Buddha-way? Why does he say that from the first attainment of Buddhahood until parinirvāṇa, in all that interval, not one word is spoken? And that the Tathāgata is always in absorption, without perception or observation? And that all Buddha-works are transformations? And that all the consciousnesses are momentary and subject to destruction? And that the vajra spirits ever follow and guard him? And that the beginning cannot be known, yet he speaks of a parinirvāṇa? And he manifests Māra and the works of Māra? And there are other retributions: the brahmin woman Sundarī, the non-Buddhist woman Cañcalā, and the return with an empty bowl, and so on. If the World-Honored One has such karmic obstructions, how can he attain the wisdom of all modes? And having attained the wisdom of all modes, how is he not free from such faults?”

The Buddha said: “Listen well, and I will tell you. Mahāmati, for the sake of the realm of nirvāṇa without residue I secretly encourage them to cultivate the bodhisattva practices. In this realm and in other lands there are bodhisattvas whose minds delight in seeking the nirvāṇa of the hearers; to make them abandon that mind and enter the great practice, I speak thus. And it is the transformation Buddha who, with transformation hearers, bestows the prediction, not the dharma-nature Buddha. Mahāmati, the bestowal of a prediction upon hearers is a secret teaching. Mahāmati, when it is said that the Buddha and the two vehicles are without difference, this is based on the single taste of liberation through cutting off the affliction-obstruction; it does not refer to the wisdom-obstruction, for the wisdom-obstruction is purified only when one sees the selflessness of dharmas. As for the affliction-obstruction, when one sees the selflessness of persons the intellect abandons it, and then the habit-energy of the ālaya-consciousness is first cut off, and only when the dharma-obstruction is liberated is it forever purified. Mahāmati, I speak this secret speech in reliance on the dharma of original abiding; it is not different from what the former Buddhas said, nor will there be further teaching afterward, for such words were already present before. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s right knowledge is without false thoughts; he does not wait to deliberate and then teach. The Tathāgata long ago cut off the four kinds of habit-energy, is free from the two kinds of death, and has removed the two obstructions. Mahāmati, the intellect, the consciousness, the eye-consciousness, and the other seven have habit-energy as their cause and are momentary in nature; apart from untainted goodness, they are not dharmas that flow on. Mahāmati, the tathāgatagarbha is the cause of the flow of birth and death and of the suffering and bliss of nirvāṇa, and the foolish, not knowing this, falsely cling to emptiness. Mahāmati, the transformation Tathāgata is ever followed and guarded by the vajra spirits; he is not the true Buddha. The true Tathāgata is beyond all measure, and cannot be known by the two vehicles or the non-Buddhists; he dwells in the bliss of the present dharma and accomplishes the forbearance of wisdom, and has no need of vajra spirits to guard him. All transformation Buddhas are not born from karma; they are not the Buddha, yet they are not other than the Buddha. Just as a potter, when various things are brought together, produces something — so too the transformation Buddha, perfect in all marks, proclaims the dharma, yet he cannot teach the realm walked by the noble wisdom of his own realization.

“Again, Mahāmati, ordinary people, seeing the six consciousnesses cease, give rise to the view of annihilation; not understanding the ālaya-consciousness, they give rise to the view of permanence. Mahāmati, one’s own mind’s discrimination is the ultimate beginning, and so cannot be known. Apart from this discrimination one attains liberation; the four kinds of habit-energy are cut off and one is free from all faults.”
“The three vehicles and those beyond vehicles — there is no Buddha’s nirvāṇa;
To all is given the Tathāgata’s prediction, and the teaching of freedom from every fault.
The accomplished and ultimate wisdom, and the nirvāṇa without residue;
To draw on the timid and the small, this secret meaning is taught.
The wisdom attained by all the Buddhas proclaims such a path as this;
This alone and nothing else — and so for them there is no nirvāṇa.
In desire, in form, in the formless, there are such views — the four kinds of habit-energy;
From these the consciousness is born, and the ālaya and the intellect are among them.
Seeing consciousness, intellect, the eye, and the rest as impermanent, they speak of annihilation;
Deluded about the intellect and the ālaya, they raise up permanence, and by wrong wisdom call it nirvāṇa.”

blocks.text: Chapter Eight: The Abandoning of Meat-Eating

inline.s: Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again spoke to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I pray you tell me the merit and the fault of eating and of not eating meat, so that I and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, having understood its meaning, may proclaim it to those beings who eat meat and are perfumed by the habits of retribution in the future and the present, and cause them to abandon the taste of meat and seek the taste of dharma; so that they may give rise to a mind of great compassion toward all beings, love one another as they would an only child, dwell on the bodhisattva grounds, and attain anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi; or, resting for a time on the grounds of the two vehicles, may at last accomplish supreme perfect awakening. World-Honored One, even the followers of Lokāyata and other non-Buddhists, who give rise to views of being and nonbeing and cling to annihilation and permanence, still forbid and do not permit the eating of meat. How much more should the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Awakened One, whose great compassion cherishes and nourishes and who is the refuge of the world, permit himself and others alike to eat meat? Excellent, World-Honored One, who are full of great compassion and pity the world, and look upon all beings as an only child: I pray you explain the faults of eating meat and the merit of not eating it, so that I and all the bodhisattvas, having heard it, may put it into practice and widely proclaim it to others.”
Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva again spoke these verses:
“Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, whose will seeks the supreme awakening;
Wine, meat, and onions too — are these to be eaten or not?
The foolish are greedy for the taste of meat, foul and without good name;
They are like those evil beasts — how then can it be eaten?
What fault has the eater? What merit has the one who does not eat?
I pray you, Supreme Honored One, fully proclaim this for me.”

Then the Buddha told Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: “Mahāmati, listen well, listen well, and ponder it well. I will explain it to you in detail. Mahāmati, all meat has countless reasons why a bodhisattva should give rise to compassion and should not eat it; I will now tell you a small part of them. Mahāmati, from beginningless time all beings have revolved without rest in birth and death, and there is none who has not been father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter, kinsman, friend, or dear attendant, and who has not taken birth again and received the body of a bird or beast. How then can one take it and eat it? Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva looks upon all beings as the same as himself, and reflects that meat all comes from something with life — how can he eat it? Mahāmati, even the rākṣasas, hearing this teaching of mine, ought to give up meat; how much more those who delight in dharma. Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, wherever he is born, looks upon all beings as his own kin, and cherishes them with compassion as an only child; therefore he should not eat any meat. Mahāmati, the meat-sellers in the streets and marketplaces, who sell the flesh of dogs, horses, men, and cattle merely for profit — how can such defilement be eaten?

“Mahāmati, all meat is formed of impure semen and blood; how can one who seeks purity take and eat it? Mahāmati, when beings see a meat-eater they are all terrified; how can one who cultivates a compassionate mind eat meat? Mahāmati, hunters, caṇḍālas, fishermen, fowlers, and other wicked people — when dogs see them they bark in fear, when beasts see them they flee, and all beings that fly in the air or dwell in the water, seeing them, think: ‘The breath of this man is like a rākṣasa’s; he has come here and will surely kill me.’ To protect their lives they all run away. So too is the meat-eater. Therefore a bodhisattva, cultivating the practice of compassion, should not eat meat. Mahāmati, one who eats meat has a foul body and a spreading evil name; the worthy and the good do not keep company with him. Therefore a bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati, flesh and blood are cast aside by all the sages and not eaten by the noble ones. Therefore a bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati, to protect the faith of beings and keep them from slandering the Buddha-dharma, a bodhisattva, out of compassion, should not eat meat. Mahāmati, if my disciples eat meat, they cause people everywhere to slander them, saying: ‘How can ascetics who practice the pure life abandon the food eaten by gods and sages, and like evil beasts roam the world with bellies full of meat, terrifying all beings, destroying the pure practice, and losing the ascetic’s path?’ Therefore you should know that in the Buddha-dharma there is no practice of taming. A bodhisattva, out of compassion for beings, to keep them from giving rise to such thoughts, should not eat meat. Mahāmati, just as burning human flesh stinks, no different from burning other flesh, how can there be eating or not eating in this? Therefore all who delight in purity should not eat meat. Mahāmati, good men and women who practice in silence in charnel grounds, beneath trees, or in solitary places, whether dwelling in a compassionate mind, or holding mantras, or seeking liberation, or tending toward the Mahāyāna — because of eating meat all their obstacles prevent accomplishment. Therefore a bodhisattva who wishes to benefit himself and others should not eat meat. Mahāmati, one who eats meat, on seeing its shape and color, has already given rise to a mind greedy for its flavor; a bodhisattva cherishes all beings as himself — how can he, seeing them, conceive the thought of eating them? Therefore a bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati, one who eats meat is forsaken by the gods; his breath is always foul; he sleeps and dreams uneasily and wakes in dread; yakṣas and evil ghosts steal his vital essence; his mind is full of terror; he eats without knowing sufficiency; he grows in sickness and easily develops sores and scabies; he is constantly nibbled by insects; and he cannot deeply give rise to revulsion toward food. Mahāmati, I have always said: ‘Whatever you eat, conceive it as the flesh of your own child.’ If this is so even of other food, how can I permit my disciples to eat meat? Mahāmati, meat is not beautiful and not pure; it gives rise to all evils and destroys all merit; it is cast aside by all sages and noble ones. How can I permit my disciples to eat it? If one says it is permitted, that man slanders me.

“Mahāmati, you should know that pure and delicious food means rice, millet, barley, wheat, and beans, sesame oil and rock honey, and the like. These were permitted by the Buddhas of the past, and are what I praise. The good men and women of my lineage, whose minds hold pure faith, who have long planted roots of goodness, who do not give rise to greed for body, life, or wealth, and who cherish all as themselves — such people should eat these, not the things loved and prized by those of evil habits and the nature of tigers and wolves.

“Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhasena, who was addicted to the taste of meat and ate all kinds of flesh. So he continued until at last he ate human flesh; his ministers and people could not bear it and all revolted, and he lost his throne and suffered great affliction. Mahāmati, Śakra, lord of the gods, because of the remaining habit of eating meat in the past, transformed himself into a hawk and pursued a dove. I was then a king named Śibi, and pitying that dove, I cut off my own flesh to ransom its life.

“Mahāmati, even Śakra, because of a remaining habit, still troubled beings; how much more those who are without shame and always eat meat. You should know that eating meat troubles oneself and troubles others. Therefore a bodhisattva should not eat meat. Mahāmati, once there was a king who rode out to hunt; his horse took fright and bolted into the mountain wilds. With no road home and no human dwelling, he roamed together with a lioness, and did a shameful deed, and children were born. The eldest was named Kāṇḍuṣa, who later became a king and ruled over seven hundred million households. Because of the remaining habit of eating meat, he would eat no food but meat; at first he ate birds and beasts, and afterward even human beings, and all the children born to him were rākṣasas. When that body ended, he was born again among lions, jackals, wolves, leopards, eagles, and vultures. Though he sought a human body, he could never attain it, much less the path of birth and death and nirvāṇa.

“Mahāmati, one who eats meat has such countless faults, and one who cuts it off and does not eat gains great merit. The foolish do not know such loss and gain; therefore I now proclaim it for you: whatever is meat should not be eaten.
