Mahāmati, those who kill living beings mostly do so for people to eat; if people did not eat, there would be no killing. Therefore eating meat and killing share the same guilt. How strange that the world, greedy for the taste of meat, will even eat human flesh — how much less will any refrain from birds and beasts. Because of greed for its taste they devise many means: nets and snares are set everywhere, and beings of water, land, and air are all killed. Even if they do not eat it themselves, they do these things out of greed for its price.

“Mahāmati, there are also people in the world whose minds have no compassion, who practice only cruelty and violence like rākṣasas. When they see a being whose body is plump, they conceive the thought of meat and say it can be eaten. Mahāmati, in the world there is no meat that is not self-slain or slain by another, and that one could eat without doubt of killing. For this reason I permit hearers to eat such meat. Mahāmati, in future ages there will be foolish people who go forth in my dharma, who falsely expound the Vinaya, corrupt the true dharma, and slander me, saying that I permit the eating of meat and that I myself once ate it. Mahāmati, if I permitted hearers to eat meat, I would not be one who dwells in a compassionate mind, who practices contemplation, who follows the dhuta practices, who tends toward the Mahāyāna. How then could I urge good men and good women to conceive toward all beings the thought of an only child and to cut off all meat? Mahāmati, where I have taught in other places that ten kinds are forbidden and three permitted, this was to gradually prohibit it and lead them to practice. But in this sūtra, whether self-slain or slain by another, whatever is meat is entirely cut off. Mahāmati, I have never permitted disciples to eat meat, nor do I permit it now, nor shall I ever permit it. Mahāmati, whatever is meat is wholly impure for one who has gone forth.

“Mahāmati, if a foolish person slanders me, saying that the Tathāgata permits the eating of meat and ate it himself, you should know that such a person is bound by evil karma and will surely fall forever into the realm of woe. Mahāmati, my noble disciples do not even eat the coarse food of ordinary people, much less the impure food of blood and flesh. Mahāmati, hearers, solitary realizers, and bodhisattvas eat only the food of dharma; how much more the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s dharma-body is not a body fed on mixed food. Mahāmati, I have cut off all afflictions, I have washed away all habit-energy, I have well chosen the wisdom of all minds, and with great compassion I look upon all beings equally as an only child. How could I permit my hearer-disciples to eat the flesh of their own children, much less eat it myself? For one who says such a thing there is no such possibility.”
“All have once been kin, grown from many impurities,
A terror to all living things — therefore it should not be eaten.
All meat, and onions, leeks, garlic, and all liquor;
Such impure things the practitioner keeps far away.
One should also always avoid sesame oil, and all beds with holes;
For the tiny insects there are greatly terrified within them.
Eating and drinking give rise to heedlessness, and heedlessness gives rise to wrong awareness;
From awareness greed is born — therefore it should not be eaten.
Because wrong awareness gives rise to greed, the mind is drunk with greed;
The drunken mind prolongs craving, and from birth and death there is no release.
For profit one kills living beings, and with wealth one takes their flesh;
Both are evil karma, and at death one falls into the Hell of Wailing.
Not thinking, not ordering, not seeking — these three are called pure;
In all the world there is no flesh like this; the one who eats it I reprove.
Devouring one another in turn, they fall at death among the evil beasts;
Foul and reeking, crazed in mind—therefore one should not eat it.
Hunters, outcastes, butchers, and rakshasas;
Born among such kinds—these are the fruits of eating flesh.
Having eaten it, one is shameless, and crazed in every life;
Hated and loathed by Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and shravakas.
The Elephant-Handled and the Great Cloud, the Nirvāṇa and the Angulimala,
And this Lankavatara Sutra—in them all I forbid the eating of flesh.
I have already taught that flesh seen, heard of, or suspected must be abandoned;
By the power of evil habit, the foolish discriminate in vain.
As greed obstructs liberation, so too do meat and the rest;
Whoever eats of them cannot enter the noble path.
In ages yet to come, beings will speak foolishly of meat,
Saying, “This is pure and blameless; the Buddha allows us to eat it.”
Even pure food should be taken as medicine, thought of as a child’s flesh;
Therefore the practitioner, knowing the right measure, goes about on alms.
Eating flesh turns one from liberation and offends the holy marks;
It strikes terror into living beings—therefore one should not eat it.
For those who dwell in loving-kindness I declare constant loathing of it;
Lions, tigers, and wolves may then keep one’s company.
If at wine and flesh and the like one never eats at all,
One is surely born among the sages, rich in wealth and in wisdom.”

At that time the Buddha said to Mahamati Bodhisattva Mahasattva: “Mahamati! The Buddhas of the past, future, and present, wishing to protect those who uphold this sutra, have all spoken the dharani of the Lankavatara Sutra. I too shall now speak it; hold it well in mind.” And he spoke the dharani, saying:

Tadyathā [1]. Tuṭha tuṭha ([tuṭha], read as “too-tah” throughout) [2]. Duṭha duṭha [3]. Paṭha paṭha [4]. Kaṭha kaṭha [5]. Amale amale [6]. Vimale vimale [7]. Nime nime [8]. Hime hime [9]. Bhāme bhāme ([bha] with the short vowel, as “bhah”) [10]. Kale kale [11]. Kārakale [12]. Aṭa maṭa [13]. Caṭa cāṭa [14]. Jñāṭa sphaṭa ([jñā] and [spha] are each two syllables) [15]. Kṛte kṛte ([kṛ], read as “krit” throughout) [16]. Bhte [17]. Hime hime [18]. Dhīme [19]. Cale cale [20]. Bali bali [21]. Bhaṇḍe vibhaṇḍe [22]. Aṃce maṃce [23]. [unclear] dha (read as “dharma” throughout) [24]. Dudha [25]. Padha [26]. Ake ake [27]. Make make [28]. Cakre cakre (two syllables) [29]. Dhi (read by its own sound) me dhime [30]. Hime hime [31]. [unclear] [32]. Chu chu chu chu (read as “chu”) [33]. Du du du [34]. Duhu duhu duhu duhu ([duhu] is two syllables) [35]. Svāhā [36].

“Mahamati! In ages yet to come, if a good man or good woman receives, upholds, reads, and recites this dharani and explains it for others, you should know that such a person will gain no foothold among all the humans, non-humans, ghosts, and spirits. If someone has suddenly met with evil, and one recites it a hundred and eight times for that person, the evil spirit will at once flee away. Mahamati! I shall speak another dharani for you.” And he spoke the dharani, saying:

Tadyathā [1]. Padmaṭṭhe [2]. Padme [3]. Hine hine hime hine ([hi], read as “he” throughout) [4]. Riju riju ([ri], read as “ree”) [5]. Huri huri [6]. Yule yule [7]. Paru paru [8]. Chinne chinne ([chin], read as “chin”) [9]. Bhave bhave [10]. Nīrakare [11]. Svāhā [12].

“Mahamati! If a good man or good woman receives, upholds, reads, and recites this dharani and explains it for others, such a one will gain no foothold among all the evil ghosts and spirits—devas, nagas, yakshas, humans, non-humans, and the rest. It is to hold back all the rakshasas that I speak this sacred dharani. Whoever holds this dharani is one who holds the Lankavatara Sutra, and all its words and phrases are thereby complete in him.”

blocks.text: Chapter Ten: The Verses, Part One of Two

inline.s: At that time the Blessed One, wishing to proclaim once more the broad meaning of this sutra, spoke these verses:
“All dharmas are unstable; they rise from discrimination,
Discrimination itself is empty; what is discriminated is not.
From false discrimination consciousness comes to be,
Eight or nine consciousnesses, various as the ocean’s waves.
Habit and tendency ever grow, deep-rooted and firmly fixed;
The mind follows its objects as iron follows the magnet.
The nature on which beings depend is free of all reckoning,
And free of what the intellect knows; by turning the basis one is freed.
One gains the samadhi of illusion and surpasses the ten grounds;
When the mind-king is seen, the notions and consciousness all withdraw.
When the mind has turned its basis, it is then the ever-abiding;
It stands within the lotus palace, risen from an illusory realm.
Dwelling in that palace, one is free and works without effort;
One benefits living beings as a mani jewel of many hues.
There is neither made nor unmade; only false discrimination is,
Which the foolish, deluded, grasp at, like a barren woman’s dream-child.
Know that the pudgala, the aggregates, realms, and conditions,
Are all empty, without own-nature, unborn, existent and yet not.
I teach by skillful means, and truly there are no marks;
Yet the foolish grasp at random the grasping and the grasped.
All knowing is not knowing, all is not all;
The foolish discriminate this, but the Buddha knows no self or other.
All dharmas are like illusion and dream, unborn, without own-nature;
Because their nature is empty, nothing is unattainable.
I teach only the one nature, apart from false reckoning;
Its own-nature has no duality; it is the walk of all the sages.
As when the four elements are disordered, one vomits and sees fireflies;
Whatever is seen is not; so too it is with all the world.
As grasses, trees, and potsherds appear through an illusion;
That illusion has no being; so too it is with all dharmas.
Neither grasping nor grasped, neither bound nor binding;
Like illusion, like a mirage, like a dream, like a film on the eye.
If one would see the real, be free of all discriminative grasp;
One should cultivate the contemplation of the real, and seeing the Buddha, doubt no more.
The world is equal to a dream, and so are form and all one’s goods;
If one can see in this way, one’s body is honored by the world.
The three realms rise from mind, seen in delusion and false imagining;
Apart from delusion there is no world; knowing this, one turns the tainted basis.
What the foolish see they falsely call arising and ceasing;
The wise see in accord with reality: neither arising nor ceasing.
Ever dwelling in non-discrimination, far from mind and mental factors;
One abides in the heaven of form’s end, beyond all fault and error.
There one attains perfect enlightenment, with powers, penetrations, and mastery;
And all the peerless samadhis are manifested and perfected here.
Transformation bodies beyond measure roam through every place,
Causing the foolish to hear the Dharma like an echo, beyond all thought.
Far from beginning, middle, and end, and free of being and non-being;
Not many, yet appearing as many; unmoved, yet everywhere.
It is taught that within the bodies of beings the covered nature is real;
Delusion makes illusion seem real; illusion is not delusion.
Because the mind is deluded, all things are taken as existing;
Bound by these very marks, the storehouse consciousness gives rise to the world.
Thus all the world is only a provisional name;
All views flow like a torrent through the dharmas of gods and men.
If one can know in this way, one turns the basis round;
Then one is my true child, one who accomplishes the Dharma in accord.
What the foolish discriminate—the dharmas solid, moist, warm, moving—
Are names without reality, with no mark and nothing marked.
Body and faculties are all made of the eight substances;
The foolish reckon form in vain, deluded by the body’s cage.
The foolish and unwise discriminate: all is born of causes and conditions;
Not understanding the mark of the real, they turn through the three existences.
The seeds within consciousness can manifest the mind’s own objects;
The foolish give rise to discrimination and reckon vainly on the twofold grasp.
Ignorance, craving, and karma—all the minds arise depending on these;
Therefore I understand it as the nature of dependence on others.
Falsely discriminating that things exist, the deluded mind goes its way;
This discrimination is wholly none; delusion vainly reckons it as being.
The mind is bound by conditions and gives rise to living beings;
When conditions are far abandoned, I say that nothing is seen.
When all conditions are left behind, and the marks of own-nature discriminated;
Within the body they no longer rise; for me there is no going.
What arises in the minds of beings—the grasper and the grasped—
Is seen to be without marks; the foolish discriminate in vain.
The alaya is revealed, the sublime storehouse consciousness;
Free of the grasped and grasper, I call it true suchness.
Within the aggregates there is no person, no self, no being;
Arising is only consciousness arising, ceasing only consciousness ceasing.
As in a painting, high and low are seen, yet nothing is there;
So too with all dharmas: they are seen, and yet they are not.
Like a city of the gandharvas, like a mirage in the heat;
What is seen is ever thus; the wise see it as unattainable.
By cause and condition and by simile the teaching is established;
The gandharva city, the dream, the fire-wheel, the mirage, sun and moon.
By the similes of the fire, the hair, and the rest, one shows the unborn;
The world’s discriminations are all empty, deluded as a dream.
Seeing that all that is does not arise, one relies on nothing in the three realms;
Within and without it is the same; one accomplishes the patient acceptance of the unborn.
One gains the samadhi of illusion and the body born of mind;
All the superknowledges and powers, and all sovereign mastery.
Dharmas by nature are unborn, empty, with no self-nature;
Deluded about causes and conditions, one says there is birth and death.
The foolish falsely discriminate: mind brings forth mind;
And brings forth outer forms as well, though truly nothing exists.
As absorption's power observes, a Buddha image and a chain of bones;
And analyzing the elements, one sets up the world by convention.
Body, possessions, and dwelling place—these three are what is grasped;
Mind-grasping and discrimination—these three are the grasper.
Deluded, one falsely reckons and clings, by grasper and grasped dividing;
Following only the realm of words, one never sees the true.
The practitioner contemplates with insight: all dharmas have no self-nature;
At that time he dwells in the signless, and all is laid to rest.
As when one paints a chicken with ink, the unwise falsely grasp it;
Truly there are no three vehicles—the foolish cannot see this.
If one sees the hearers, and the pratyekabuddhas too;
They are all great compassion bodhisattvas, appearing through transformation.
The three realms are only mind, discriminating two natures;
With the support turned, free of person and dharmas, this is suchness.
Sun, moon, lamplight and flame, the elements and the mani jewel;
They act without discrimination—so too do all the Buddhas.
All dharmas are like a hair-net, far from arising, dwelling, and ceasing;
They are also free of permanence and impermanence; defilement and purity are likewise so.
As one who takes the taduttha drug sees the ground as golden;
Yet truly within that ground there is no mark of gold at all.
The foolish are likewise so: with mind deluded since no beginning;
They falsely grasp all things as real, as illusion, as a mirage.
One should observe a single seed as sealed the same as non-seed;
One seed is all seeds—this is called the mind's variety.
The seeds are one, and the turning of the support is the non-seed;
Equal, the same dharma-seal, wholly without discrimination.
The many and various seeds can bring forth birth in all the destinies;
The many and mingled sufferings—this is named all the seeds.
Observing the self-nature of all dharmas, delusion needs no dispelling;
The nature of things is unborn; to know this is liberation.
One in absorption observes the world: all forms arise from the mind;
With mind deluded since no beginning, truly there is no form and no mind.
Like illusion and a mirage city, a hair-net and a shimmering haze;
They are not existent yet appear to be—so too are all dharmas.
No dharma is ever born; it is only what delusion sees;
Since they arise from deluded falsity, the foolish vainly reckon two.
Through all the various habitual tendencies, waves of mind are born;
When those habits are cut off, the waves of mind no longer arise.
The mind arises in dependence on objects, as a painting rests upon a wall;
If not, then in empty space, why does no painting appear?
If it is by a share of marks and features that the mind is made to arise;
Since the mind arises from conditions, the meaning of mind-only does not hold.
The nature of mind is intrinsically pure, like the stainless sky;
That the mind again grasps the mind is due to habit, no other cause.
Clinging to what one's own mind displays, one makes the mind arise;
What is seen is truly not outside—therefore it is taught as mind-only.
The storehouse consciousness is called mind; thinking is held to be mentation;
That which knows all the objects of sense is then named consciousness.
Mind is ever neutral; mentation has two kinds of action;
The present consciousness is complete in both, the wholesome and unwholesome and the rest.
When one realizes it, there is no fixed time—one transcends the grounds and all the lands;
One also passes beyond the measure of mind, and dwells in the fruit of the signless.
What is seen as existent and nonexistent, and all the various marks;
Are all clung to, inverted, by the foolish.
If wisdom is free of discrimination, things existing would be contradicted;
Through mind there is therefore no form; hence there is no discrimination.
The sense faculties are like illusions; all their objects are like dreams;
The agent and the act—all of them do not exist.
In conventional truth all things exist; in the highest meaning, nothing does;
The no-nature of all dharmas is taught as the highest meaning.
Within no self-nature, because of all verbal conventions,
Things do arise—this is named conventional truth.
If there were no verbal convention, the things that arise would not be either;
In conventional truth there is no one who speaks and yet has no thing.
Inverted and false dharmas are truly ungraspable;
If the inverted were existent, then there would be no absence of self-nature.
Because they are without existence and nonexistence, those inverted dharmas;
And all that is owned—none of it can be grasped.
Evil habits perfume the mind, and all the various marks appear;
Deluded, one says they are outside the mind, and falsely grasps all the forms.
Discrimination and non-discrimination—discrimination can be cut off;
By non-discrimination one can see, realize the true nature, and attest true emptiness.
Ignorance perfumes the mind, and all the beings appear;
Like phantom elephants and horses, and leaves of trees taken for gold.
As one with a clouded eye, deluded, sees a hair-net;
The foolish are likewise so, falsely grasping all the objects.
The discrimination, what is discriminated, and the one who brings forth discrimination;
The turning, what is turned, and the cause of turning—by this cause there are six liberations.
Because of false reckoning, there is no ground and no truths;
Nor are there any Buddha-lands, transformation Buddhas, or the two vehicles.
Mind brings forth all dharmas, every place, and the body;
The nature of mind is truly signless, yet the unwise grasp at variety.
The marks of discrimination and delusion are named the dependent arising;
The names that are within the marks are then the false reckoning.
When conditions and dharmas come together, and one discriminates names and marks,
None of these is ever born—this is the perfectly accomplished nature.
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, among beings and bodhisattvas,
All the Dharma-body and reward-body Buddhas, the transformation bodies and their changes,
All issue forth from Amitāyus, from within the realm of Ultimate Bliss;
In the Vaipulya scriptures, one should know, this is spoken with hidden intent.
Whatever the Buddha's sons have taught, and whatever the guides have taught,
All of it is the teaching of transformation bodies, not the true reward-body Buddha.
No dharma is ever born, yet neither is it nonexistent,
It is like an illusion, like a dream, like a phantom, like a mirage city.
The many varieties arise from mind, and by mind the many varieties are freed;
Mind arising is nothing else besides; the ceasing of mind is likewise so.
Because beings discriminate, false and deceptive marks appear;
Mind-only truly has no object; free of discrimination, one is released.
Through beginningless accumulation, one discriminates all the idle theories;
Perfumed by evil habits, this false and deceptive object arises.
Because one falsely reckons a self-nature, all dharmas are unborn;
Resting upon dependent arising, beings are deluded and discriminate.
When discrimination no longer accords, the dependent is itself pure;
Dwelling free of discrimination, the turning of the support is just suchness.
Do not falsely reckon the false; false reckoning is without reality;
Deluded and falsely discriminating, both the grasped and the grasper are none.
To discriminate and see an outer object is the falsely reckoned nature;
From this false reckoning, the nature of dependent arising is born.
With wrong views about outer objects: there is no object, it is only mind;
Observing rightly in accord with principle, both grasper and grasped are extinguished.
As the foolish discriminate, an outer object truly does not exist;
Habitual tendencies disturb and muddy the mind, so it turns as if an outer object were there.
The two discriminations being extinguished, wisdom accords with suchness;
It arises free of any image—inconceivable, the range of the noble ones.
Relying on the union of father and mother, like butter within a jar;
The ālaya and the mental, together joined, make the red and white to grow.
The arbuda and the peshi, from defiled karma born in many ways;
The karma-wind swells the four great elements, and birth comes forth as fruit that ripens.
Five and five and five, and nine kinds of sores and apertures;
With nails and teeth and hair complete, when all is full, then birth takes place.
The newborn is a worm in dung, and like a man awakening from sleep;
The eyes open and see forms, and discrimination gradually grows.
When discrimination has been decided through, the lips and palate join and meet;
Then speech begins to issue forth, just like a parrot and the rest.
Following the dispositions of all beings, one establishes them in the Great Vehicle;
That is no ground for evil views; the sectarians cannot accept it.”
“The vehicle realized within oneself is no range for reckoning thought;
Pray tell: after the Buddha’s passing, who will be able to uphold it?”
“Mahāmati, you should know that after the Sugata’s nirvāṇa,
In future ages there will be those who hold to my Dharma.
In the land of South India a bhikshu of great renown and virtue;
His name is Nāgārjuna, who will shatter the schools of being and non-being.
He will make known in the world my Supreme Great Vehicle;
He will attain the first Ground of Joy and be reborn in the Land of Bliss.
Things arising from conditions: neither being nor non-being is tenable;
In conditions the fool imagines a thing, and discriminates being and non-being;
Views such as these of the sectarians stand far apart from my Dharma.
The names of all dharmas ever follow upon their place of birth;
Both what has been habituated and what is now habituated, each turns and discriminates with the other;
If one does not speak of names, the whole world would be bewildered;
To dispel bewilderment, therefore, names and words are established.
The foolish discriminate all dharmas, deluded by names and words;
And so too the conditioned arising of all things: these are the three kinds of discrimination.
Because it neither arises nor ceases, its own nature is like space;
Its self-nature is nothing at all: this is called the mark of vain imagining.
Like illusion, shadow, mirage, mirror-image, dream, and fire-wheel;
Like echo and like a phantom city: this is the dependent arising.
Suchness, emptiness, non-duality, the real limit, and the dharma-nature;
All of these are free of discrimination: this I call the perfected nature.
The range of language and of mental factors falls falsely into the two extremes;
Wisdom discriminates the ultimate truth; that wisdom is free of discrimination.
To the wise it appears, to the foolish it appears not;
Thus what wisdom reveals: all dharmas are without marks.
Like a necklace of counterfeit gold, not gold, yet the fool calls it gold;
So too are all dharmas: the sectarians vainly reckon and measure.
All dharmas have no beginning and no end, abiding in the mark of the real;
The whole world is uncreated: the vainly imagining cannot comprehend it.
Whatever dharmas there were in the past, and in the future and the present;
All dharmas such as these are entirely unborn.
Because conditions come together, therefore things are spoken of as existing;
If one is free of that coming-together, there is no arising and no ceasing.
But in dharmas arisen from conditions, neither sameness nor difference can be found;
Spoken of briefly, they are arising; spoken of at length, they are cessation.
The one is the emptiness of the unborn, and the other is the emptiness of the born;
The emptiness of the unborn is supreme; the emptiness of the born is decay and ruin.
The various bodies born of the will, I say, are merely different names.
With regard to all the sutras, vinayas, and treatises, a pure discrimination is stirred up;
If one does not understand selflessness, one relies on the teaching and not on the meaning,
And beings vainly discriminate, seeing what is like a hare’s horn,
Discrimination itself is delusion, like a thirsty beast pursuing a mirage.
Through false attachment and grasping, discrimination is stirred up;
If one is free of the cause of false grasping, discrimination does not arise.
The profound and vast and wide: to know the sovereign freedom of all lands;
I speak this for the Buddha’s sons, and not for the śrāvakas.
The three existences are empty and impermanent, far removed from self and what belongs to self;
For the śrāvakas I speak in just these general terms.
Not clinging to any dharma, dwelling alone in still quiescence;
Thinking on the fruit of the pratyekabuddha, I speak thus for those beings.
The body is dependent arising, yet delusion does not see itself;
It discriminates an outer self-nature, and so makes the mind falsely arise.
The fruit of karmic reward, empowerment, and the births of every kind of realm;
And what is obtained in dreams: these are the four natures of the superknowledges.
What is obtained within a dream, and by the Buddha’s awesome power;
The births of every kind of realm and the rest are not the superknowledge of karmic reward.
Habitual tendencies perfuming the mind bring forth appearances like things;
The common and foolish cannot awaken to this, and so it is spoken of as arising.
Following along with vain discrimination, how long do outer marks endure?
For just so long delusion grows, and one does not see that one’s own mind is deluded.”
“Why is it taught that there is arising, and not that there is what is seen?
Seeing without anything seen, for whom and how could it be taught?”
“The essence of mind is itself originally pure, though joined with the mental and all the consciousnesses;
Because habitual tendencies ever perfume it, it becomes all manner of turbidity and confusion.
The storehouse consciousness abandons the body, and the mental seeks the various realms;
Consciousness is deluded into seeming objects, and having seen them, grasps them with greed.
What is seen is only one’s own mind; no outer object can be found;
If one cultivates such contemplation, one casts off vain thinking and accords with suchness.
The range of those in samādhi, of karma, and of the Buddha’s awesome power;
These three are inconceivable, the range of the inconceivable wisdom.
The past and future pudgala, space, and nirvāṇa;
I follow the conventions of the world; the ultimate truth is free of letters.
The two vehicles and the sectarians alike rely upon and rest in views;
Deluded about mind-only, they vainly discriminate outer objects.
The arhat and the pratyekabuddha, and the bodhi of the Buddhas;
The seed firmly accomplished: a Buddha appears in a dream and sprinkles them with water.”
“The illusion of mind tends toward stillness: why is being and non-being spoken of?
Where, and for whom? For what reason? Pray explain it for us.”
“Because of delusion about mind-only, being and non-being are spoken of as illusion;
Arising and ceasing answer to one another, and mark and marked are equal.
Discrimination is called the mental consciousness, together with the five consciousnesses;
Like images and a torrent, they arise from the seeds of the mind.
If the mind and the mental, and all the consciousnesses, do not arise;
Then one attains the body born of the will, and also reaches the Buddha-ground.
The various conditions, the skandhas, and the realms, and the own-marks of person and dharmas;
Are all mere mind-made designations, like a dream and a hair-net.
Seeing the world as illusion and dream, one rests upon the real;
The real is free of all marks, and free too of corresponding causes.
What the noble ones realize within, ever dwelling in no-thought;
Delusion answers to causes, and so grasps the world as real.
When all vain talk is extinguished, delusion then does not arise;
Wherever there is deluded discrimination, a foolish mind ever keeps appearing.
All dharmas are empty and without nature, and yet are ever and not ever;
This is the view of those who propound arising, not the doctrine of the unborn.
Sameness, difference, both, and neither; nature and sovereign lord;
Time, atoms, and primal matter: conditions discriminating the world.
Consciousness is the seed of birth and death; because there is a seed, there is birth;
As a painting depends upon the wall, so when one understands, it at once ceases.
Just as one sees an illusory man, and there is illusory birth and death;
So too are the common and foolish: through delusion bondage and release arise.
The two kinds of dharmas, inner and outer, and their conditions;
The practitioner observes, and they all abide in signlessness.
Habitual tendencies do not leave the mind, nor do they dwell together with it;
Though the mind is entwined by habit, the mind’s mark has no distinction.
The mind is like a white garment; the habits of consciousness are the grime;
Soiled by the stains of habit, they keep the mind from showing forth.
I say it is like space: neither existing nor non-existing;
The ālaya too is just like this: both being and non-being it flees.
When consciousness turns and takes new reliance, the mind is free from turbid confusion;
This mind I call the Buddha, for it awakens to every dharma.
Forever cut are the three continuities, and the four propositions left aside;
Both being and non-being are cast away, for all existences are forever like illusion.
The first seven stages arise from the mind, and so a twofold nature springs;
Upon the remaining stages, and the Buddha's, perfect truth is seen.
The realms of desire, of form, and of no-form, and also nirvāṇa—
all the bodies there are the mind's own domain.
Whenever something is gained, just then does confusion arise;
but when one has awakened to one's own mind, confusion does not arise.
I establish two kinds of dharma: the marks, and the realization;
by four modes of reasoning, as means, I set forth the accomplishment.
To see the various names and marks is deluded discrimination;
when one is free of names and marks, one dwells in the stainless nature.
Following the discrimination of grasper and grasped, the imagined mark appears;
when one is free of that discrimination, one dwells in the nature's own.
When the mind is liberated, it is everlasting and true;
the buddha-nature and the dharma-nature, and suchness, hold no discrimination.
Because there is a mind that is pure, defilement is seen to appear;
with no purity there is no defilement: true purity is what the noble ones tread.
The world arises from conditions, and grows through discrimination;
beholding it as illusion and dream, one is at that moment freed.
The manifold evil habitual tendencies are commingled with the mind;
and so beings see an outer realm, and never behold the mind's own nature.
The mind's nature is intrinsically pure, and gives rise to no confusions;
confusion rises from evil habit—and therefore one does not see the mind.
Confusion itself is the real; the real is nowhere else;
for the formations are no formations, and are seen nowhere else.
If one beholds all that is conditioned, far from the grasped and the grasper,
then, by being free of every mark, one sees the world as mind alone.
Abiding securely in mind-only, one discriminates no outer realm;
one dwells upon the object that is suchness, and passes beyond the mind's own measure.
When one has passed beyond the mind's own measure, one passes beyond the markless too;
for one who dwells in the markless cannot see the Great Vehicle.
With action stilled and effort spent, one purifies the great vows;
and because it is markless, my own supreme wisdom is not seen.
One should behold what the mind ranges over, and behold what wisdom ranges over;
beholding what insight ranges over, one is not confused about marks.
What the mind ranges over is the truth of suffering; what wisdom ranges over is its origin;
the remaining two truths, and the Buddha-stage, are all what insight ranges over.
The winning of the fruit and of nirvāṇa, and the noble eightfold path,
and the awakening to every dharma—this is the Buddha's stainless wisdom.
The eye as faculty, the field of form, space, light, and the turning of attention—
by these, from out the ālaya, beings' eye-consciousness is born.
The grasper with the grasped and grasping, name and thing—all are nothing at all;
and to discriminate without a cause—this is what the unwise do.
Name and meaning do not give birth to one another, and name and meaning are not separate either;
to reckon that things arise from a cause, or from no cause, is never free of discrimination.
The fool says he abides in the ultimate truth, and speaks as his views decree;
but a single nature with five, thus it cannot be—so let the truth's meaning go.
Those who prattle of being and non-being—one should pass beyond such demons;
for having seen there is no self, one no longer craves existences.
Those who reckon the maker to be permanent, with spells and wrangling ways;
the ultimate truth is beyond all speech, and in it one beholds the quiescent dharma.
Relying upon the ālaya, therefore, the manas comes to turn;
and because mind and manas are its reliance, the various consciousnesses are born.
The dharmas that false imagining posits, and the mind's own nature of suchness—
thus does the man of samādhi contemplate, and comprehends the nature that is mind-only.
He contemplates the manas with the marks and their affairs, and thinks not of permanent or impermanent;
nor of arisen or unarisen—he discriminates neither of the two.
From out the ālaya there arise the various consciousnesses;
yet never upon a single meaning do two kinds of mind arise.
Because he sees his own mind, it is neither empty nor speakable;
but if one does not see one's own mind, one is bound in the net of views.
The conditions have no arising; the faculties have no existence;
there is no greed, no aggregate or element—nothing conditioned at all.
Deeds and their rewards were never there; there is no making, nothing made;
attachment was never there to begin with, so there is no bondage and no more.
There is no neutral dharma either, and neither dharma nor non-dharma;
there is no time, no nirvāṇa—the dharma-nature cannot be grasped.
It is not Buddha, not the ultimate truth, not a cause and not a fruit;
not an inversion, not nirvāṇa, not arising and not passing away.
Nor are there the twelve links, nor the extremes and the non-extremes;
every view is wholly cut away—and this I call mind-only.
Affliction, karma, and the body, and the fruit that karma yields;
all are like a flame, like a dream, like a city of the gandharvas.
Because one dwells in mind-only, all the marks are left behind;
because one dwells in mind-only, one can see both severance and permanence.
In nirvāṇa there are no aggregates, no self, and no mark;
by entering into mind-only, one wins liberation through the turning.
Because evil habit is the cause, the great earth appears as outer;
and so too all living beings—yet in mind-only nothing is seen.
Body, wealth, and land are images shown forth by beings' habits;
the mind is neither being nor non-being, but habit-energy keeps it hidden.
Stain appears within the pure, not purity within the stain;
as clouds obscure the open sky, so the mind does not appear.
The imagined nature one takes as existing, yet in dependent arising it is not;
through the deluded clinging of the imagined, dependent arising holds no discrimination.
Not everything made is form, and there is form that is not made;
dream-form, mirage-form, flame-form: these are not made at all.
If, regarding dharmas born of conditions, one calls them real or unreal,
such a one will surely rest upon the views of oneness and of difference.
Hearers are of three kinds: those born of aspiration and of transformation,
and those whose greed and hatred are gone—the ones born of the dharma.
Bodhisattvas too are of three kinds, not yet having a Buddha's marks;
thinking upon living beings, they manifest the Buddha's form.
Whatever is manifested by beings' minds arises all from habitual tendencies;
the manifold various images, like stars and clouds, the sun and moon.
If the great elements truly existed, then something made could arise from them;
but since the great elements have no nature, there is no grasper and no grasped.
The great elements are the maker, and earth and the rest are what is made;
but the great elements were never born, and so no made form exists.
The imagined and the real, and every form, and forms the illusion makes—
dream-form, mirage-form, and flame-form, which is the fifth.
The icchantikas are five in kind, and the lineages as well;
five vehicles and no vehicle, and nirvāṇa of six kinds.
The aggregates are twenty-four, and forms are of eight kinds;
the Buddhas are twenty-four, and the Buddha-sons are of two.
The dharma-gates are a hundred and eight, and the hearers are of three;
the Buddhalands are but one alone, and the Buddha likewise one.
Liberation is of three kinds, and the mind's outflows are four;
selflessness is of six kinds, and the knowables also four.
Far removed from any maker, and from every kind of view;
inner self-realization, unmoved—this is the supreme Great Vehicle.
The born and the unborn: of these there are eight kinds and nine;
in a single instant or by stages, the realized goal is one.
The formless realm has eight kinds, and the dhyānas differ sixfold,
the solitary buddhas and the Buddha-sons: deliverance is sevenfold.
In the three times nothing at all exists, nor permanent and impermanent;
Deeds and their ripening fruits are all as things seen in a dream.
The Buddhas are from the first unborn, yet appear as hearers and Buddha-sons;
The mind can never behold them, for all dharmas are like illusions.
Therefore in every land they descend from Tuṣita and enter the womb;
Their first birth and their going forth are not born from a place of birth.
For beings adrift in the stream, they speak of nirvāṇa;
The truths and the lands, according to each one's capacity, they cause to awaken.
The continents, trees, and groves of the world, selflessness, and the sectarians' ways;
The vehicle of Chan and the ālaya: their fruition and their objects are inconceivable.
The kinds of stars, moons, and constellations, and the lineages of kings and gods;
The kinds of gandharvas and yakṣas are all born through karma and craving.
The inconceivable death of transformation still keeps company with the habitual tendencies;
When death is utterly exhausted, the net of afflictions is already cut.
Wealth and grain, silver and gold, fields and houses and servants,
Elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep: none of these should one keep.
One should not lie on a couch with holes, nor plaster the ground with mud,
Bowls of gold, silver, or copper: none of these should one keep.
Vessels of clay, stone, iron, crystal, and beryl,
Filled to the measure of a Magadha bushel: these are allowed as bowls.
With colors such as blue, with cow-dung, mud, fruits, and leaves,
One dyes white and other cloths, making them the color of the saṃghāṭī robe.
A knife of four finger-breadths, its blade shaped like a half-moon,
Is allowed to the practitioner for cutting out and sewing his robe.
Do not study the arts and crafts, nor should one buy and sell;
If need arises, employ a lay attendant: this is the Dharma I have taught.
Always guard the sense faculties, and well understand the sense of sutra and vinaya;
Keep no intimacy with worldly folk: such a one is called a practitioner.
Beneath trees, in rocky caves, in huts in the wild, and among the tombs,
In huts of grass and in open ground, there the practitioner should dwell.
Among the tombs and in other places, keep the three robes always with you;
If robes should be lacking, what a donor brings one should accept.
Going out to wander for alms, look only a yoke's length ahead;
Gathering in the thoughts, one begs for alms as a bee takes nectar from a flower.
Where crowds are gathered in tumult, and where bhikṣuṇīs mingle promiscuously;
Where livelihood is made, and where one consorts with the worldly, one should not beg at all.
Kings and princes, ministers and elders:
The practitioner begging for alms should hold none of them close.
Houses of birth and houses of death, houses beloved of kin and friends,
Houses where monks and nuns are jumbled together: the practitioner does not eat there.
Where the kitchen smoke never ceases and all manner of dishes are always cooked,
And where food is purposely prepared for oneself: the practitioner does not eat there.
The practitioner contemplates the world as the perceiving marks and the marks perceived;
Both of these are wholly free from birth and death, and free as well from being and non-being.

blocks.text: Chapter Ten, Part Two: The Verses

inline.s: If practitioners do not give rise to discrimination,
Before long they attain samādhi, the powers, the spiritual penetrations, and mastery.
The practitioner should not vainly cling to the view that things arise from atoms,
From time, from a sovereign nature, or from a creator, as the cause of the world.
The world arises from one's own discrimination, born of various habitual tendencies;
The practitioner should contemplate all existence as a dream, an illusion.
Ever dwelling far from both denigration and affirmation;
As to body, possessions, and dwelling place, one does not discriminate the three realms of existence.
Without thought of food or drink, one sits upright, mindfully, body steady;
Again and again one bows in reverence to the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas.
Well understanding the sutras and the vinaya, the Dharma of true meaning and purport;
The five dharmas and the two kinds of selflessness, and likewise one ponders one's own mind.
Inner realization of the pure Dharma-nature, the stages, and the Buddha-ground;
The practitioner who cultivates this is consecrated in the lotus.
Sinking and turning through all the destinies, one grows weary of all existence;
Repairing to a quiet place among the tombs, one cultivates the various contemplations.
That things arise without a cause, they vainly claim, is free of annihilation and permanence;
They also claim it is free of being and non-being, and vainly reckon this the middle way.
Vainly reckoning a doctrine of no cause, their no-cause is the view of annihilation;
Not understanding outer things, they destroy the middle way.
Fearing to fall into the view of annihilation, they do not relinquish the dharmas they grasp;
By affirming and denigrating, they vainly proclaim the middle way.
Awakening to mind-only, one abandons outer dharmas;
One also leaves vain discrimination: this practice accords with the middle way.
Mind-only has no object; where there is no object, mind does not arise;
I and all the Tathāgatas declare this to be the middle way.
Whether arising or not arising, self-nature or no self-nature;
Being, non-being, and the like are all empty; one should not discriminate the two.
Unable to give rise to discrimination, the fool calls this liberation;
If no knowing awareness arises in the mind, how can one cut off the two grasping?
By awakening to one's own mind, one can cut off the two grasped-at objects;
Through knowing one can cut them off; it is not that one cannot discriminate.
Knowing that all is manifested by the mind, discrimination no longer arises;
Because discrimination no longer arises, the mind of true suchness is transformed in its basis.
If one sees the dharmas that arise as free of the faults of the sectarians;
This is what the wise grasp: nirvāṇa is not destruction.
I and all the Buddhas teach that awakening to this is itself Buddhahood;
If one discriminates otherwise again, that is the doctrine of the sectarians.
Unborn yet appearing to be born, unceasing yet appearing to cease;
Everywhere in all the billions of lands, they appear at once like the moon in water.
One body becomes many bodies, kindles fire, and pours down rain;
Appearing in each mind according to its capacity: therefore it is taught as mind-only.
The mind too is mind-only, and what is not mind also arises from mind;
All the various forms and marks, thoroughly understood, are mind-only.
The images of the Buddhas, the hearers, and the solitary realizers;
And all the other various forms are all taught to be mind-only.
From the formless realm down to the hells;
All that appears for beings is entirely the work of mind-only.
The illusion-like samādhis, and the mind-made bodies;
The ten stages and sovereign mastery are all gained through the transformation of the basis.
The fool is bound by marks, following seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing;
His own discrimination is inverted, stirred by vain talk and play.
All is empty and unborn; I in truth do not enter nirvāṇa;
Manifested Buddhas in every land set forth the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
The Buddha has thirty-six kinds, and each of these again has ten;
According to the vessels that are beings' minds, he manifests the various lands.
The Dharma-Buddha in the world is like the nature of vain reckoning;
Though various things are seen, in truth there is nothing at all.
The Dharma-Buddha is the true Buddha; all the rest are manifested Buddhas;
According to the seeds in beings, one sees the bodies the Buddha manifests.
Because of confusion about the various marks, discrimination arises;
Discrimination is not different from the true, yet marks are not themselves discrimination.
Self-nature, enjoyment, and transformation bodies, and transformations again manifested from these;
The thirty-six qualities of the Buddha are all accomplished by self-nature.
From seeds perfumed by outer things, discrimination is born;
One does not grasp the real, but grasps what is falsely clung to.
Confusion rests on the inner mind and takes outer objects as its condition;
It arises from these two alone; there is no third condition.
Confusion rests on inner and outer, and having thus arisen;
Sixty and twenty-eight: therefore I speak of it as mind.
Knowing that there are only faculties and objects, one is free of the grasping of self;
Awakening to the mind as having no object, one is free of the grasping of dharmas.
Because of reliance on the foundational consciousness, the various consciousnesses arise.
Because of reliance on the inner sense-bases, semblances of outer images appear;
The unwise ever discriminate the conditioned and the unconditioned,
Yet none of them can be grasped, as in a dream, a star, or a hair-net.
Like a city of gandharvas, like illusion, like water in a mirage,
Not existing yet seeming to exist—so too are dharmas of dependent arising.
Relying on three kinds of mind, I speak provisionally of faculties, objects, and self;
Yet those minds and consciousnesses have no self-nature whatsoever.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness—selfless, and of two kinds;
The five dharmas and self-nature are the realm of all the Buddhas.
Habit-energy is their single cause, and from it the three marks are formed;
As with a single color, one paints a wall and sees many things.
The five dharmas and the two selflessnesses, self-nature, mind, and consciousness—
Within the Buddha lineage, all of these are wholly unattainable.
Far removed from mind and consciousness, and apart from the five dharmas;
Apart again from self-nature—this is the Buddha lineage.
If by body, speech, and mind one cultivates not the pure white dharmas;
The Tathāgata’s pure lineage is then far from manifestation.
Sovereign in the powers of superknowledge, adorned by pure samādhi,
The various mind-born bodies—these are the Buddha’s pure lineage.
Inwardly self-realized and stainless, far removed from marks of cause,
The eighth ground and the Buddha ground are formed by the Tathāgata nature.
Far-going and Good Wisdom, the Dharma Cloud and the Buddha ground;
All these are the Buddha lineage; the rest are included in the two vehicles.
The Tathāgata’s mind is sovereign, yet for all the foolish folk,
Because the mind’s marks differ, he speaks of seven kinds of ground.
On the seventh ground there arise no faults of body, speech, or mind;
The eighth ground’s reliance is like a dream, like crossing a river.
The eighth ground and the fifth ground comprehend the crafts and sciences;
The Buddha’s sons can become kings among all that exist.
The wise do not discriminate whether born or not born,
Empty and non-empty, self-nature and no self-nature—
These are but measures of the mind, and truly unattainable.
For the two vehicles he teaches: this is real, this is false;
Not so for the Buddha’s sons—therefore one should not discriminate.
Existence and non-existence are both unreal, and no mark of an instant is found;
Conventional and real dharmas are likewise none—only mind, ungraspable.
Dharmas that exist are conventional truth; the absence of nature is the supreme meaning;
To be deluded about that absence of nature—this is the worldly view.
All dharmas are empty; for the common and the foolish,
I set them forth provisionally, following the world—yet these have no reality.
The dharmas that arise from words have meanings they seem to convey;
But seeing what words give rise to, one finds it all unattainable.
As without a wall there is no painting, without substance no shadow;
If the storehouse consciousness is pure, the waves of the consciousnesses do not arise.
From the dharmakāya there is the reward body; from the reward arises the emanation body;
This is the root Buddha; all others are what emanation manifests.
One should not falsely discriminate emptiness and non-emptiness;
Falsely reckoning existence and non-existence, the meaning of words is unattainable.
The common and foolish falsely discriminate the real qualities of atoms gathered into form;
Each and every atom is none—therefore there is no object.
The outer marks that beings see are all manifested by their own minds;
Since what is seen does not exist, there are no outer objects at all.
Like an elephant sunk in deep mud, unable to move again;
The śrāvaka abiding in samādhi is mired and bogged just the same.
If one sees the world with habit-energy as its cause;
Beyond existence, non-existence, and both—in the selflessness of dharmas there is release.
Imagined nature is false reckoning; dependent arising is the other-dependent;
Suchness is the perfected—this I constantly teach in my sutras.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness, discrimination and expression;
The root consciousness makes the three realms—all are other names for mind.
Lifespan, warmth, and consciousness, ālaya and the life faculty;
Intellect and consciousness—all are other names for discrimination.
The mind can sustain the body; the intellect ever weighs and ponders;
Consciousness together with all the consciousnesses cognizes the mind’s own object.
If a self truly existed, apart from the skandhas or within them;
Seeking that self there, one finds it utterly unattainable.
Observe the world one by one: it is all one’s own mind appearing;
From the afflictions and their latency, one is freed from suffering and released.
The śrāvaka has the wisdom of exhaustion; the pratyekabuddha, the wisdom of stillness;
The Tathāgata’s wisdom arises without end or limit.
Outwardly there is truly no form—it is only what one’s own mind manifests;
The foolish do not know this, and falsely discriminate the conditioned.
Not knowing that outer objects of every kind are all one’s own mind;
The foolish establish them by reasons and analogies, through the four propositions.
The wise fully comprehend that objects are one’s own mind appearing;
They do not establish them by tenets, reasons, analogies, or any propositions.
Discrimination and the discriminated—this is the mark of false reckoning;
Resting upon false reckoning, discrimination arises once again.
They lean on one another in turn, all from a single habit-energy;
These two are both but guests; they do not arise from beings’ minds.
Dwelling at ease within the three realms, mind and mental factors discriminate;
The seeming objects that arise are the imagined self-nature.
Images and seeds together make the twelve sense-fields;
When support and object join, one speaks of deeds that are performed.
Like an image in a mirror, like hairs seen by a clouded eye;
So too when habit-energy covers, ordinary folk give rise to false views.
Toward the objects of one’s own discrimination, discrimination then arises;
As the sectarians discriminate—outer objects are unattainable.
As the fool, not knowing a rope, seizes it falsely as a snake;
Not knowing the mind’s own appearing, he falsely discriminates outer objects.
Thus the rope’s own body is apart from both sameness and difference;
It is only the mind’s inverted delusion that falsely raises the rope-discrimination.
When one falsely reckons and discriminates, that nature is not there;
How is it that, seeing what is not, discrimination arises?
The nature of form is nothing at all, and so are pot and cloth;
They arise only from discrimination; what is seen in the end does not exist."
"Amid beginningless conditioned existence, confusion gives rise to discrimination;
What dharma causes the confusion? May the Buddha speak it for me."
"All dharmas have no self-nature; they are only what the mind manifests;
Not comprehending one’s own mind, one therefore gives rise to discrimination.
As the foolish discriminate and falsely reckon, it truly does not exist;
What exists otherwise than this, they are unable to know.
What the noble ones possess is not what the foolish discriminate;
If the noble were the same as the common, the noble would have falsity.
Because the noble one governs and purifies the mind, there is no confusion;
The common and foolish mind is impure, and so false discrimination arises.
As a mother speaks to her infant: you need not weep and wail;
Fruits will come down from the sky, and you may take them, all kinds, as you please.
For beings I teach the fruits of every kind of false reckoning;
Having made them love and delight in it, the Dharma truly transcends existence and non-existence.
All dharmas were at first non-existent, their conditions not yet joined;
What was unborn appears as born, and has no self-nature at all.
An unborn dharma does not arise; apart from conditions there is no place of birth;
So too with dharmas now arising—apart from conditions they are unattainable.
Observing the essential truth of dependent arising: neither existing nor not existing;
Not existing, not non-existing, not both—the wise do not discriminate.
The foolish folk among the sectarians falsely speak of sameness and difference;
They do not comprehend dependent arising: the world is like illusion, like a dream.
My unsurpassed Great Vehicle transcends words and names;
Its meaning is most clear, yet the foolish do not awaken to it.
What the śrāvakas and sectarians teach is all stingy and withheld;
They make the meaning all distorted—all of it arising from false reckoning.
All marks and self-bodies, their shapes and their names—
Clinging to these four, all manner of discriminations arise.
They reckon Brahmā or Īśvara makes them, one body or many;
or that the sun and moon so move — such a one is no child of mine.
One who is fully possessed of noble vision, who comprehends the Dharma as it really is,
who deftly turns about all his notions, has reached the farther shore of consciousness.
By this seal of liberation he forever leaves behind existence and nonexistence;
and freed from coming and going, such a one is a child of my Dharma.
If form-consciousness were to turn and cease, and the various karmas were to be destroyed,
then there would be no birth and death, and no permanence and no impermanence.
Yet when that turning and ceasing takes place, though the realm of form is cast aside,
karma abides in the ālaya, free from the faults of existence and nonexistence.
Though form-consciousness turns and ceases, karma is not destroyed;
it causes form-consciousness to continue again throughout the various realms of existence.
If the karma produced by those sentient beings were to be destroyed,
then there would be no birth and death, nor would there be nirvāṇa.
If karma and form-consciousness were to perish together at the same time,
then in birth and death, when birth occurs, form and karma would not be distinct.
Form, mind, and discrimination are neither different nor not different;
the foolish speak of their destruction, yet in truth they transcend existence and nonexistence.
Dependent arising and false imagining have no marks distinct from each other;
as with form and impermanence, so too does each arise from the other.
Since they are apart from difference and non-difference, false imagining cannot be known;
like the impermanent nature of form, how can one speak of existence or nonexistence?
One who fully understands false imagining sees that dependent arising does not arise;
by seeing dependent arising, false imagining itself is suchness.
If one destroys the imagined nature, one destroys the eye of Dharma;
and so, within my Dharma, one sets up assertions and slanders it.
People of such a kind will slander the true Dharma;
by what is not Dharma they destroy the eye of my Dharma.
The wise should not speak with them, nor share a monk's affairs;
for by destroying false imagining they establish it and slander it.
If one follows after discrimination and gives rise to views of existence and nonexistence,
such a one is like an illusory hair-net, a dream, a mirage, or a gandharva city.
Such a one does not learn the Buddha's Dharma, and should not be dwelt with;
for he falls into the two extremes himself and ruins others as well.
If there is a practitioner who contemplates the imagined nature,
in stillness apart from existence and nonexistence, one may receive him and dwell with him.
Just as in the world there are places where gold and maṇi gems are found;
though there is no maker there, sentient beings still make use of them.
So too is the nature of karma, far removed from all kinds of natures;
the karma one sees is not existent, yet it is not that the realms are not born.
As the noble ones have understood it, all dharmas are without any own-being;
but the dharmas that the foolish discriminate and falsely imagine are not nonexistent.
If those dharmas that the foolish discriminate were in fact nonexistent,
then since all dharmas are absent, sentient beings would have no defilement.
Yet because there are defiled dharmas, bound by ignorance and craving,
one can give rise to a body of birth and death, with all the faculties complete.
If one says that all these dharmas discriminated by the foolish are nonexistent,
then the faculties would not be born, and that is not right practice.
If these dharmas did not exist as the cause of birth and death,
the foolish, without waiting to practice, would be liberated of themselves.
If those dharmas did not exist, how would the ordinary and the noble differ?
Nor would there be noble ones practicing the three liberations.
The aggregates, the person, and dharmas, in their own and common marks, are markless;
the various conditions and the faculties — these I teach for the śrāvakas.
Mind-only, the non-cause, the stages, and Īśvara;
the inwardly realized, pure suchness — these I teach for the Buddha's children.
In ages yet to come there will be those who wear the kāṣāya robe,
who falsely speak of existence and nonexistence and destroy my true Dharma.
Dependent arising is without own-nature; this is what all the noble ones practice;
the imagined nature is a thing apart, discriminated by those who calculate.
In times to come there will be fools, the Khaṇḍa and other heretics,
who teach the doctrine of no cause, whose wrong views ruin the world.
They falsely declare that all the worlds arise from minute atoms;
and that those atoms have no cause, that the nine kinds of substance are permanent.
From the real comes the real, from the quality is born the quality;
the nature of true Dharma is other than this, yet they slander it and call it nonexistent.
If what was not came to be, the world would then have a beginning;
but birth and death have no beginning — this is what I teach.
If all things in the three realms arose from what was not,
then camels, donkeys, and dogs would grow horns, and of that there could be no doubt.
If eye, form, and consciousness, which were not, now come to be,
then clothes, caps, and mats should be born from a lump of clay.
Just as there is no mat in the reed, and no mat in the bulrush,
why should not a mat be born from each and every one of the conditions?
If the life-principle and the body arise from what was not,
then, as I have said before, all such views are the talk of heretics.
The doctrines I have taught before were set forth to refute their meaning;
and having refuted them, I then teach my own doctrine.
Lest the assembled disciples be deluded and cling to the doctrines of existence and nonexistence,
therefore I first set forth for them the doctrines of the heretics.
Kapila, of evil wisdom, taught his disciples
that the primordial nature gives rise to the world, transformed by the guṇas.
Since the conditions are nonexistent, there is no already-born and no presently-born;
since the conditions are not conditions, there is neither arising nor non-arising.
My doctrine is apart from existence and nonexistence, and apart from all causes and conditions;
arising and ceasing, and the marks they produce, are all entirely left behind.
The world is like an illusion or a dream; causes and conditions are all without own-nature;
always contemplating thus, discrimination never arises again.
If one can regard all that exists as a mirage or a hair-net,
or as a gandharva city, one forever stands apart from existence and nonexistence.
Abandoning causes and conditions altogether, one makes the mind entirely pure;
if one says there is no external object, and that there is only mind.
Without an object there is no mind — how then is mind-only established?
Because there is an object to be perceived, the minds of sentient beings arise.
Without a cause the mind does not arise — how then is mind-only established?
Suchness and mind-only are what all the noble ones practice.
One who says this exists but that does not does not understand my Dharma;
it is from the grasped and the grasper that the mind comes to arise.
The worldly mind is like this, and so it is not mind-only;
body, possessions, land, and images arise from the mind as in a dream.
Though the mind takes on two parts, the mind has no two marks;
as a blade does not cut itself, as a finger does not touch itself.
And the mind does not see itself — so too is this matter;
where there is no image, there is no dependent arising.
The imagined nature too is absent; the five dharmas and the two minds are exhausted;
the producer and the produced are both marks of one's own mind.
It is by hidden intent that the producer is taught, and in truth there is no own-nature;
if the various shapes of objects were born from false imagining,
then space and a rabbit's horn should also become objects;
but since the object arises from the mind, this object is not falsely imagined.
Yet that falsely imagined object cannot be found apart from the mind;
throughout beginningless birth and death, objects are entirely nonexistent.
The mind has no place from which it arises — how then are images formed?
If something could arise from nothing, a rabbit's horn should also arise.
Nothing can arise from nothing, giving rise to discrimination;
just as an object appearing as nonexistent was nonexistent before as well.
How, in a state without objects, could the mind arise toward an object?
Suchness, emptiness, the real limit, nirvāṇa, and the dharma realm —
all dharmas are unborn; this is the nature of the highest meaning.
The foolish fall into being and non-being, discriminating various causes and conditions.
They cannot know the manifold existences—unborn, and with no maker;
The ground of the beginningless mind: mind alone, and nothing seen.”
“Since there is no beginningless object, from what could mind arise?
If a thing arises without anything, the poor should be rich.
If mind arises without an object, I pray the Buddha will explain it to me;
If all is without a cause, then there is neither mind nor object.”
“Since mind itself is unborn, it is free from the three realms and their making;
It is by way of the jar, the cloth, and the horn that one says the rabbit’s horn is not.
Therefore one should not say that the dharmas of those marks have no cause;
Where being has no cause, it is not; and that non-being is not established as non-being.
So too with the dependent: without it, likewise; they arise in mutual dependence;
If one thing depends upon another, then some other thing arises.
Then that which is depended upon first would exist of itself without a cause;
And if that has yet another support, that support too has a support.
Thus it would be endless, and not a single dharma would exist;
As illusions appear in many forms depending on wood and leaves,
So it is with beings: by depending on things, all manner of things appear;
By the power of the magician, the foolish see illusory forms.
Yet in the wood and the leaves no illusion at all is to be found;
But if it depends upon a thing, then this dharma is destroyed.
Since what is seen is not two, how could there be any discrimination?
In discrimination there is no false imagining, and discrimination itself is not.
Because discrimination is absent, there is no birth-and-death and no nirvāṇa;
Since there is nothing discriminated, discrimination does not arise.
How is it that mind does not arise, and yet mind-only is established?
The distinctions of the mental are immeasurable, yet none of them is real;
There is no reality and no liberation, and no worlds at all;
Whatever the foolish discriminate is not to be found outside.
Habit-energy disturbs and muddies the mind, so that it appears like images;
All dharmas of being and non-being are altogether unborn.
They are only what one’s own mind displays, utterly apart from discrimination;
The teaching that all dharmas arise from conditions is for the foolish, not for the wise.
The mind’s own nature is liberated; the pure mind is where the noble ones dwell;
The Sāṃkhyas, the victorious ones, and the naked ascetics, the brahmins and the Īśvara-worshippers,
All fall into the view of non-being and stray from the meaning of stillness;
Unborn, without own-nature, stainless and empty, like an illusion.”
“The Buddhas and the present Buddha—for whom do they speak thus?
For the cultivator of the pure mind, who is free of all views and conjectures.”
“The Buddhas speak for such as these, and so do I;
If all is mind, where does the world abide?
For what reason is the great earth seen, and beings coming and going,
Like birds roaming through space, following after discrimination?
Without support and without abiding, they walk as though treading the earth;
So it is with beings: they follow false discrimination.
They course through their own mind as a bird moves through space;
The images of body, wealth, and land—the Buddha teaches that they arise from mind alone.”
“Pray tell us of the image that is mind-only: by what cause, and how, does it arise?”
“The images of body, wealth, and land all turn about through habit-energy.
They also arise from discrimination that is not in accord with principle;
The outer object is a false imagining, and the mind arises taking that object as its condition.
When one understands that the object is mind-only, discrimination does not arise;
If one sees the nature of false imagining, name and meaning do not coincide.
Apart from the perceived and the perceiving, one is freed from all that is conditioned;
When name and meaning are both abandoned—this is the Dharma of the Buddhas.
If one seeks awakening apart from this, one has no awareness of self or other;
If one can see the world as free from the perceived and the perceiving,
Then there arises no discrimination of the name and the named;
Because one sees one’s own mind, false names and words cease.
Not seeing one’s own mind, one gives rise to that discrimination;
The four aggregates have no form or mark, and their number cannot be got.
The great elements differ in nature—how do they together produce form?
Because they are free of all marks, the made and the maker are not.
If form apart from form had a mark, why would the aggregates not arise?
If one sees the markless, one abandons both aggregates and sense-fields.
Then the mind too is free, because one sees that dharmas are without self;
From the differences of faculties and objects, the eight kinds of consciousness are born.
Within that which is without marks, these three marks are all abandoned;
The mental consciousness, taking the ālaya as its object, gives rise to the grasping of self and mine.
And when one knows that the two graspings of consciousness are all abandoned,
One contemplates and sees freedom from unity and difference, and so is unmoved.
Free from self and mine, the two kinds of false discrimination
Are unborn and without increase, and are not the cause of consciousness.
Since the made and the maker are abandoned, once ceased they do not arise again;
The world has no maker, and is free from the marks of maker and made.”
“Pray explain to us false imagining and mind-only.”
“One’s own mind displays all manner of things, and one discriminates their various forms;
Not understanding what the mind displays, one falsely grasps it as outside the mind;
Through unwise awareness, one gives rise to the view of non-being.
How is it that toward existing things the mind does not become attached?
One discriminates neither being nor non-being, and so does not arise toward being.
Understanding that what is seen is mind-only, discrimination does not arise;
Because discrimination does not arise, the support is turned and one clings to nothing.
Thus one sets aside the four theses—that dharmas have a cause, and the like;
These are but different names; none of what they posit is established.
One should know that the maker-cause too is not established;
To set aside the maker, one speaks of the concurrence of causes and conditions.
To set aside the fault of permanence, one says conditions are impermanent;
The foolish say impermanent, but in truth there is no arising or ceasing.
One does not see any dharma of destruction that can do anything;
How could an impermanent dharma be able to produce anything?
Devas, humans, asuras, ghosts, beasts, and Yama’s realm, and the rest—
Beings are born among them; this I call the six paths.
By karma high, middling, and low, they receive birth among them;
Guarding all good dharmas, one attains the supreme liberation.”
“The Buddha has spoken to the monks of the births they receive;
Thought after thought, all is arising and ceasing—pray expound this for me.”
“Form after form does not pause, and mind after mind too arises and ceases;
For my disciples I teach that the thoughts they receive pass away and change.
In form after form there is discrimination, and in arising and ceasing likewise;
Discrimination is beings; apart from discrimination they are not.
For this reason I teach the arising of thought after thought;
If one is free of the grasping that holds to form, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
The conditioned and the unconditioned, ignorance and suchness, and the rest—
Because of the two dharmas there is arising; without the two, there is suchness.
If that conditioned and unconditioned, the dharmas of arising, are different,
Then permanence and the like, together with the conditions, would have maker and made.
That is what the Great Muni and all the Buddhas have taught;
But to have a maker and a made is no different from the non-Buddhists.
For my disciples I teach that the body is the suffering world;
It is also the world’s origination, and cessation and the path are all complete.
Because ordinary folk falsely discriminate and grasp the three natures,
They see a grasped and a grasping, in worldly and transcendent dharmas alike.
Because I first contemplated dependence, I spoke of grasping at own-nature;
Now, to set aside all views, one should not falsely discriminate.
To seek faults is not the Dharma, and it leaves the mind unsettled;
All this arises from the two graspings; without the two, there is suchness.
If ignorance, craving, and karma give rise to consciousness and the rest,
Then false thoughts must have a cause, and that is the fault of endlessness.
The unwise speak of all dharmas, and there are four kinds of destruction;
When false twofold discrimination arises, dharmas are in truth beyond existence and nonexistence.
Beyond the four propositions, from the two views apart;
The twofold born of discrimination, once known, is born no more.
In what is unborn one knows birth, in birth one knows the unborn;
Because those dharmas are equal, one should not give rise to discrimination.”
“May the Buddha tell me the principle that refutes the two views;
So that I and the rest of the assembly may never fall into existence or nonexistence.”
“Not mingled with the sectarians, and beyond the two vehicles;
What the Buddhas have realized and practiced is where the Buddha's sons do not fall back.
Liberation is neither cause nor non-cause, one and the same unborn mark;
Deluded, one clings to different names; the wise should always keep far from them.
Dharmas are born of discrimination, like a hair-wheel, an illusion, a mirage;
The sectarians vainly discriminate that the world arises from a self-nature.
The unborn, suchness, emptiness of nature, and true reality;
These are taught as different names; one should not cling to them as nonexistence.
As a hand has many names, so too does Indra have many names;
So too are all dharmas; one should not cling to them as nonexistence.
Form is not different from emptiness, and the unborn is the same;
One should not cling to them as different: that brings the fault of every view.
By discriminating the general and the particular, and by all-pervading discrimination;
One clings to the marks of all things, long and short, square and round.
Discriminating the general is mind, all-pervading discrimination is manas;
Discriminating the particular is consciousness, all beyond the marks of grasped and grasper.
To give rise to views within my Dharma, and the non-arising of the sectarians;
Both are false discrimination, their faults equal and no different.
If one can understand the non-arising that I have taught;
And what non-arising is for, that person understands my Dharma.
To break every view, non-arising dharmas have no dwelling place;
That these two meanings may be known, I teach the Dharma of non-arising.
If the non-arising I teach were existence or nonexistence;
It would be one with the sectarians' doctrine of non-arising without cause.
What I teach is the measure of Mind-only, far removed from existence and nonexistence;
Whether it be birth or no birth, such views should all be abandoned.
The doctrine of no cause does not arise; where there is birth, one clings to a maker;
With a maker, views are mixed; without one, things arise of themselves.”
“The Buddha teaches all skillful means, right view, the great vows, and the like;
If all dharmas were nonexistent, how could the seat of enlightenment be won?”
“Free from the grasped and the grasper, neither born nor ceasing;
The dharmas and non-dharmas one sees all arise from one's own mind.”
“What the Sage has spoken is at odds with itself;
How can he teach all dharmas and then speak of non-arising?
Living beings cannot understand; may the Buddha explain it for me;
That we may leave the sectarians' fault and their cause of inversion.
May the Supreme Teacher proclaim both birth and cessation;
All free from existence and nonexistence, yet without destroying cause and effect.”
“The world falls into the two extremes, deluded by all its views;
May the Blue-Lotus-Eyed One teach the stages of the grounds in order.
Grasping at birth and no birth, one does not know the cause of quiescence;
At the seat of enlightenment nothing is gained, and I too have nothing to teach.
Momentary dharmas are all empty, unborn and without self-nature;
The Buddhas have purified duality; to hold two is itself a fault.”
“Covered by wrong views, one discriminates—that is not the Tathāgata;
Vainly reckoning birth and cessation, may he explain it for us.”
“Accumulated through idle talk, born of concordant conditions;
Each appears before its kind, and form-objects are all complete.
Having seen outer forms, one gives rise to discrimination;
If one can understand this, then one sees the true meaning.
If the great elements were absent, no thing could be produced;
The great elements being Mind-only, know that nothing is born.
This mind too is unborn; then one accords with the noble lineage;
Do not discriminate discrimination; non-discrimination is wisdom.
To discriminate discrimination is duality, not nirvāṇa;
To posit a thesis of non-arising destroys the dharmas of illusion.
And without a cause illusion cannot arise, so one's own thesis is diminished;
Like an image in a mirror, which is free from the one and the different.
What is seen is not nonexistent, and the mark of birth is likewise;
Like a city of the gandharvas or an illusion, all await causes and conditions to exist.
So too are all dharmas: this is birth, not non-arising;
One discriminates a person and dharmas, and so gives rise to two kinds of self.
This is but worldly talk, and the foolish do not know it;
By vows and gathered conditions, by self-power and by the Supreme;
The fifth is the doctrine of the hearers, and there are arhats and the like;
Time, interval, and destruction, ultimate meaning and succession.
These four kinds of impermanence the foolish discriminate, and they are not wisdom;
The foolish fall into the two extremes: the qualities, the atoms, a self-nature as maker.
Clinging to the doctrines of existence and nonexistence, they do not know the cause of liberation;
The great elements oppose each other—how could they give rise to form?
